E. ARTHUR HAGLUND

E. ARTHUR HAGLUND
Grand Master

October 12, 1983-0ctober 11, 1984

One Mason Can Make a Difference-You!
Thus did Grand Master E . Arthur Haglund espouse this philosophy
throughout the year as he traveled up and down the State of California
and on his visitation to the State of Hawaii. By his enthusiasm , spirit ,
dedication and persuasiveness he convinced all who heard him that here
was one Mason who did indeed make a difference .
Recognizing many of the problems besetting our Fraternity, he instituted programs aimed at achieving quality and excellence in the operation
of the individual Constituent Lodge. Along with these new programs, long
term goals and objectives were defined and plans formulated to accomplish them. Working in conjunction with the other members of the Executive Committee of Grand Lodge, improved training methods for the
benefit of Lodge officers were instituted through the Fraternal Management Course as well as an expansion of the Leadership Workshops for all
interested Masons.
He initiated the "Grand Master's Achievement Award ," a flexible goaloricnted recognition program for the individual Lodge , sixty-one of whom
earned this coveted award during the Grand Lodge year. He most effectively applied to the operation of the Grand Lodge his organizational ,
problem solving and management development skills developed through
many years of experience as an executive in corporate management.
Convinced that effective communication is absolutely essential for every
organization, he wrote monthly messages which were sent to each Master.
These , along with special periodic communications, we re also forwarded
to Grand Lodge Committeemen and District Inspectors. A planning workshop was held for groups of Committee Chairmen. and two special seminars were conducted for all District Inspectors concerning Grand Lodge
programs and their non-ritual responsibilities . Direct mailings were sent
to the entire membership of our Jurisdiction as were additional messages
in the quarterly publication of the California Freemason Magazine . The
purpose of all these was to inform all Masons of this Jurisdiction not only
of the philosophy of the Grand Master and to identify the programs as
they developed or were emphasized throughout the year, but also to emphasize the concerns of our Jurisdiction and to impress on each individual
Mason his responsibility in helping turn upward our serious downward
membership and participation trends.
Our Grand Master was born in Havre , Mo ntana where his fathe r,
brother and grandfather were active Masons. As a youth he was active in
DeMolay, his church and the Boy Scouts as well as football, band, cho rus
and other activities in school. He is a Past Master Councilor of Havre
Chapter, Order of DeMolay and holder of the Chevelier Degree. He is
an Eagle Scout with four palms and was awarded the "God and Country
Award." Married to the vivacious and lovely Barbara Jean, also a native
of Montana , this delightful couple have two married children and three
grandchildren.
Art is a veteran of the United States Navy. He graduated from the
University of Montana with a Bachelor of Science Degree in Business
Administration and completed graduate ~chool in production management
iii

at the University of Washington. Having served Kaiser Aluminum for
some thirty years, during which time the Haglunds lived in Washington ,
West Virginia, Ohio as well as California, our Grand Master chose to
retire , thus completing a most successful professional career in management positions in computer syste.ms, financial planning and production
planning and control.
His Masonic career began on January 21, 1969 when he was initiated
an Entered Apprentice Mason in Acalanes Lodge No. 723 (now AcalanesFellowship No. 480). Raised to the Sublime Degree of Master Mason on
June 24, 1969, he served as Master during the year 1978. He was a Trustee
on the Masonic Homes Board prior to his election in October of 1980 as
Junior Grand Warden, in October of 1981 as Senior Grand Warden and
in October of 1982 as Deputy Grand Master. In October of 1983 he was
elected and installed as the 118th Grand Master of Masons in California
and Hawaii. His Masonic membership includes the Scottish and York
Rites, Shrine , National Sojourners , High Twelve, the Royal Order of Scotland , and he has been elected to membership in the Order of Knights of
the Red Cross of Constantine.
Our Grand Master's sincere conviction is that Masonry needs a high
profile in order to grow and regain significance in our society. He had
installed in each Masonic Temple throughout the Jurisdiction display racks
for pamphlets and brochures on Masonry including two new ones , not
only for the edification of our membe rs but for the general public as they
use our various Temple facilities. In addition , he promoted Masonic festivals which the general public might attend and also encouraged Masonic
participation in County Fairs through the use of Masonic Information
booths. Under his direction, short T. V. "spots" were developed and distributed to television stations throughout the Jurisdiction , emphasizing
Masonic involvement in the United States Constitution as well as our
Observance programs and the rehabilitation of the Statue of Liberty. Both
emphasize a need for responsibility and our commitment to the form of
government under which we live aJong with the .patriotism we feel for our
country.
Our retiring Grand Master can look back upon his Masonic endeavors
with the full knowledge that his many contributions to our great Frate rnity
were most beneficial and will long be remembered. May he and Barbie
enjoy every blessing that life can afford no matter where their travels may
take them in the coming years.
One Mason CAN make a difference! You!

Freemasonry is the oldest institution of its kind and, as such , has been
blessed by the great Providence of our God in guiding our Fraternity
through many difficult and perilous periods of world and national history.
It is my conviction that , while recognizing the benefits of this Divine
Guidance , we also have an equally great responsibility to respond with a
deep commitment to the continual challenge of truly touching the hearts
and minds of me n with the God-given principles of our Fraternit y.
Men, perhaps as never before, are hungry for truths which Masonry has
to offer. They face unce rtainties and pains and losses in our world today;
they sense the inner battles within themselves ; they seek for answers; they
seek desperately for the means to achieve peace , strength and courage .
They can find direction for their lives in the truths of Masonry if Masonry
will rise to its triumphal potential.
Where do we find these truths? The open Bible on the Masonic altar
is God's powerful searchlight. It records man's search for God and God's
quest for man . Psalm 119 tells us that "Thy word is a lamp unto my fe et
and a light unto my path." The Bible is our textbook of faith and practice
that forms the basis of Masonic principles, the great light in our profession ,
the unerring standard of truth and justice by which we regulate our behavior and our attitude toward our brothers and sisters in the world. In it
we learn the important duties which we owe to God. our neighbor and
ourselves.
Placed in perspective the Sacred Law teaches us about the Fatherhood
of God and the Brotherhood of Man which are the basic purposes of all
true Masons. 1 believe it is important that, shining through the impressive
ritualistic performance in our Lodges, the great light of brotherly love ,
kindness, patience and faith must be reflected through the symbols and
teachings of the' degree work if the ultimate objectives of Masonry are to
be reached .
It is important that men today acknowledge the Power greater than
themselves , the Supreme Being, Great Architect, Designer, Creator of all
the worlds of our universe both known and unknown, the Author of Everlasting Life , the God of all people of every nation.
To be aware of the Fatherhood of God is to know that, underlying all
the superstructure of our personal , social and political life is the fou ndation
of an eternal and loving God whose laws of justice , mercy, temperance ,
prudence, forgiveness and love are constant, never-changing and dependable; the Supreme Being who seeks to govern the events of history through
the Sacred Law challenges men to pursue the pathway tha t leads to the
good life, to do good for all mankind and to be true to those principles
that assure freedom and justice for all. To acknowledge the Fatherhood
of God is to be reminded that "men do not live by bread alo ne" and that
the important possessions of life are not material but spiritual. The Holy
Writings reaffirm this:

Devotional Message
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
I am grateful for this rare privilege which is mine this morning to share
my personal thoughts of faith with you at the beginning of this l35th
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Masons in California and
Hawaii.

"The Lord is my strength and my shield; my heart trusts in
Him and I am helped." "The Lord is the strength of my life ,
of whom should I be afraid?" " God is my refuge and a very
present help in trouble."

It is very important that contemporary men, Jiving in today's world,
know more about the Fatherhood of God. I say to you, my Brothers: "Let
your light so shine before men that they may see your good work and then
glorify your Father which is in Heaven."
The Bible also teaches us about the Brotherhood of Man. "Thou shalt
love the Lord thy God with all your heart, soul and mind and thou shalt
love your neighbor as yourself." We arc taught to regard the whole human
species as one family, the high and the low, the rich and the poor who, as
created by one Almighty Parent, and inhabitants of the same planet, are
to aid, support and protect each other. True Brotherhood leads us to
relieve the distressed of all men , but particularly our Masonic Brothers,
to sooth the unhappy, to sympathize with their misfortunes, to restore
peace to troubled minds.
Brotherhood is expressed very practically in every Lodge meeting when
you extend the hand of friendship , literally, to the Brothers you don't
know so well, getting acquainted with them, showing your concern for
them and their families . This friendly atmosphere in the Lodge room will
help each person to know that he is accepted and included, and he will,
in turn, be more active in his Fraternity.
Brotherhood means that we maintain open and continuous contact with
the widows of our departed Brothers , providing them social and fraternal
pleasure and helping in those very difficult months and years of adjustment
when it is important to know that someone cares.
Brotherhood means that each of us individually, and as a Fraternity of
Lodges, will give adequate support and encouragement to our Children's
Home in Covina and to our Adult Horne in Union City as our expression
of caring for those boys and girls, men and women, who find genuine
nurturing and concern in these family settings, staffed by caring people.
Brotherhood means to take righteous pride in the knowledge that for
59 years the concordant bodies of Masonry have improved the quality of·
life for a quarter million children who have been critically burned or
crippled and have discovered hope for the future through the nineteen
orthopedic hospitals and three burn institutions or for the increasing numbers of little children who might otherwise remain educationally crippled
and suffering for a lifetime but have been befriended by the Aphasia
clinics and now may talk, read and live useful lives.
Brotherhood means that we will be bold enough at times to risk the
reaching out through our Masonic youth groups to young men and women
whose need for acceptance from their peers often leads them into some
precarious lifestyle such as occurred in an East Los Angeles ghetto some
years ago when a 14 year old Navajo Indian lad, just nine years away from
his native reservation, was apprehended in the act of stealing hubcaps
from a shiny Cadillac which was parked in front of a house where a party
for so-called square kids was in progress. Out of the darkness a big hulk
of a man appeared, picked up the young lad by the nap of the neck and
began a lecture on the do's and don'ts of having a good time.
"I want to show you what a really good time is and it ain 't taking
hubcaps." Whereupon h e escorted the young man into a Halloween party
of DeMolay and Job's Daughters, many of them from his same school

across the tracks. Before long they were telling him about D eMolay and
about Dad Ashford, who took the boy to school the next day, introduced
him to the vice-principal of the school , also a Mason, who signed a petition
to join DeMolay which the boy had completed earlier. This young man
finally joined DeMolay and, as he de scribes it, his life was turned around
180 degrees. That 14 year old Navajo Indian lad, now a grown man, sits
today as a Senior Grand Steward of our Grand Lodge and who h as worked
every year of his new life with DeMolay, Rainbow, Job's Daughte rs. Blue
Lodge and in the Eastern Star Chapter where he and his wife serve as
Worthy Matron and Worthy Patron this year. He says with genuin e sincerity, "I will probably not finish paying off this debt until I meet. t he
Great Architect." All of this happened because Dad A shford a nd Atwater
Chapter of DeMolay cared enough about a young ma n who got caught up
in a confused set of values and goals. I a m convinced that we have not
extended the reach of our youth groups far enough to touch and change
the lives of teenagers in a similar dest ructive lifestyle. This may seem like
a big order, but listen to th is story:
An old man walked on the beach at dawn and noti ced a yo ung
man ahead of him picking up starfish and flinging them into
the sea. Finally catching up with the lad, he aske d him wh y he
was doing this. The answer was that the stranded starfish wou ld
die if he left them until the morning sun shined on them. " But
the beach goes on for miles and there a re millions of starfish;
how can your effort make any difference?" The young ma n
looked at t he starfish in his hand and t hen threw it to safety in
the water ; he looked up at the face of the old man with a sense
of satisfaction and replied. "It makes a difference to this o ne ."

.

My Brothers . this to me is the essence of brotherly love and relief.
Believing so much in the Fathe rhood of God for all people, young and
old, and in the Brotherhood of Man that we tak e time , e ne rgy and o ur
material wealth to m a ke the road just a little smoother for those who need
and wa nt a true brother and friend. Our society is attracted to places today
whe re they sense some genuine earing. It is my hope and prayer that our
Fraternity will increasingly find exciting new possibilities for exemplifying
the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man to our Brother M asons and to the boys and me n of our communities so that we not say only
that "we are Masons and this is what we believe" but that o thers will see
the spirit of our Fraternity in such a way as to say, " They are Maso ns and
that is how they live."
It is in that spirit that our Memorial Committee will share their words
of comfort and faith as we reme mber o ur Brother Masons who h ave been
called to that Celestial City in the Great Beyond this past year.

a very sincere and meaningful praye r.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

EULOGY
IRA WINN COBURN, P.G. M.

By Chester R . MacPhee, P.G.M.
We are gathered now, in love and in reverence of the transition of a
fine, honorable man, Ira Winn Coburn, beloved husband of Barbara Co·
burn, and devoted brother of Dorothy O 'Rear. He was an outstanding,
highly regarded , building contractor in this city for almost 50 years .
By every standard that a man may be judged , Bud Coburn earned the
never ending affection and indeed the veneration of his fellow man.
His allegiance to his beautiful Christian Science religion and to the
Masonic Order were of oak and rock and as lasting as steel and mortar.
The giving of himself for others was just as natural for Bud as it was
for him to smile-and who can ever forget that warm smile, the strong
handclasp , that chuckle , and th e continuing interest he had in us-yes, in
each o ne of us. All of this and more are a living legacy which he leaves
to those who loved him.
Masons are taught the importa nce of brotherly love amo ng all mankind,
and I am well within the mark when I say Bud Coburn added to the total
sum of love and indeed to the brotherhood of man .
Born in this great City of St. Francis on January 4, 1904, he was ed ucated in Lick-Wilmerding High School and graduated from the University
of California in the class of 1925. At the University he was selected as a
member of Delta Kappa Epsilon , and his election to four separate ho nor
societies were in recognition of his great service above self.
Preside nt and Chairman of the Board of the construction firm which
bea rs his name , he was also President of Olivet Memorial Park and Preside nt of the California Masonic Memorial Temple Associatio n.
Bud Coburn truly was a builder. He built buildings, he built character
and he built a Masonic structure within himself of honor and decency. H e
built for all to see and for a ll to benefit.
He was a builder of men- a builder of Masons.
In his hands the Square and Compass-the trowel , level. plumb , or
gavel-all were familiar tools to build a building or to build character. He
chose both.
His Masonic career began in 1930 when he was elected a member of
Do ric Lodge No. 216. He served his Lodge faithfully and was elected
Master in 1939 and Inspector in 1941.
The outbreak of war brought a change from one type of leadership to
another. Enlisting in the U. S. Army Engineers, he served his country
with distinction in the South Pacific and retired at War's end with the rank
of Lieutenant Colonel.
He subsequently resumed his active participation in Masonry and for
m any years gave valuable leadership in almost every area of the Masonic
Craft.

IRA WINN COBU RN
Grand Maste r
October 12, 1962-0ctober 18. 1963
BORN
J anuary 4, 1904
San Francisco. California

DIED
Februarv 26. 1984
San Francis~o, California

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

13

Honored with the 33rd Degree of the Scottish Rite and the Legion of
Honor of DeMolay, he was Past Sovereign of the Order of the Red Cross
of Constantine , as well as a former member of the Governing Board of
the Shriners Hospital and an Honorable Knight Templar of Golden Gate
Commander y No. 16. In the year 1962 the men of Masonry in this State
gave him their highest honor possible-th at o f Grand Master of Masons
in California and Hawaii . Once again, in this capacity, his sincerity of
purpose and sound business acumen , together with his great love for his
fellow man , brought additional honor to the Grand Lodge of Masons in
this State of California.
It was just a few months ago that his beloved Doric Lodge honored him
on his 80th Birthday. Lauded by Masonic and City officials, the tributes
paid him were well earned by his continuous service to others throughout
the years.
My friends, we have lost a great leader, not only to Freemasonr y but
to our beloved City and State and all of its people.
The older I become , the more convinced I am that life and death are
one. Imperceptib ly they blend into one another. Someone once said- " lf
there be a design in this world , there must be a designer." We know that
God is Love-more than this we cannot ask-higher we cannot lookfarther we cannot go. Yes, man 's life in this world is but a preparation for
the future. It was Father Giovanni in 1513 who said, "There is a radiance
and glory in darkness if we could but see-and to see, we have only to
look ."
Faith is the key, my friends. We go as far as we can through knowledge ,
experience and reason and then we travel the rest of the way down the
road on faith alone. That faith tells us- the spirit rises out of the grave ,
that the spirit canflot be held by flesh alone-that matter has no life to
lose and that the spirit will never, neve r die.
Angelo Patri had this to say-"ln one sense there is no death . The life
of a soul on earth lasts beyond his departure. You will always find that
life touching yours-the voice speaking to you-that spirit looking out of
other eyes. H e lives on in your life and in the lives of all others that knew
him."
My friends, it is our great privilege to come together today and acknowledge the good that came into our lives because we knew a nd were
a part of the life of Bud Coburn.
But perhaps Shakespeare said it best when he wrote-"Hi s life was
gentle and the elements so mixed in him that nature might stand up and
say to all the world, ' Now, there was a man'."
Our hearts are heavy as we gather today in this Memorial Service; but
in our faith we know that life does not end in physical death-rath er we
move from the limitations and matte r of this life to the freedom of life
eternal.
And so, among the thousands who loved him so dearly, we have come
together in love, to say a temporary farewell-sa fe in God's assurance that
we shall all surely meet again. Speech cannot contain our love. There was,
there is, no more honorable or finer man.

Memorial Devotional
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
We of this Fratern ity are of many creeds, but we are one in our be lief
in the Supreme Architect of the U niverse and in Life Eve rlasting and that
G od has prepared a place for us in a House not made with hands but
which is eternal in the Heavens.
The me mory of o ur de parted Brothe rs leaves us saddened and lonely
but as me n of faith we are not de vastated by cynicism , ange r at God fo r
their depa rture or afra id of tha t experience called Death , fo r we believe
that God 's love surrounds us in every adventure o f life and death and that
we a re a ble to commit the souls of our Brothe r Masons to the love a nd
care of our Heavenly Father. We gain reinforcement for our faith by these
words which 1 paraphrase from Psalm 23 of the O ld Testament:
"The Lord is o ur Shepherd , we shall not want
He makes us to lie down in green pastures.
He leads us beside the still waters.
He restores o ur souls.
Even though we wa lk through the valley of the
shadow of death we will fear no evil
For Thou art with us.
Thy rod and Thy staff they comfort us.
Surely, goodness and mercy shall follow us all the days of
our life , and we will dwell in the
House of the Lord forever."
It is in this unwave ring faith in the God o f our Fathers that I ask you
now to join our voices in singing the ancient hymn of faith , "H ow Great
Thou Art". Worshipful Davis Leonard will sing the verses of the hymn
and we will fill this vast auditorium with our own strong voices of faith as
we sing the chorus . We will be acco mpanied by our Grand Organist , Worshipful Ja mes Myers, and by the trumpeter, E dward Maita. Please stand
and grasp the hand of the person ne xt to you as a symbol of our unity as
Masonic Brothers and me n of faith .

GRAND MASTER 'S ACHIEVE MENT AWARD

REPORT OF THE CRAND TREASURER

During this past year Grand Master Haglund instituted a new Grand
Lodge program entitled, "Grand Master's Achieve ment Award Program."
61 Lodges earned sufficient points to qualify to receive a most handsome
and suitably engraved plaque. To confer the proper recognition that earning this award merits, the Master o r represe ntative fro m each of these 61
Lodges was escorted into the Grand Lodge by the Grand Marshal and
each was individually presented with the appropriate plaque by Grand
Master Haglund as testimo ny to the fact that their Lodge had earned this
coveted award . Following these presentation s, the Brethren accorded
these Lodges a standing ovation.

The membership statistical table to be found in this report reveals that
during the past year our J urisdiction again suffered a substantial net loss in
me mbe rs. You will note that the net loss for t he year e nding June 30, 1982
was less than for th e prior year and the net loss for the year ending June
30, 1983 agai n was less than for the prior year. lt was hoped that thi s trend
would continue; however, sad to say. our loss for this past year exceed ed
the two prior years and is the second highest net loss for any year in our
history.
Our files contain the records of several thousand candidates who are in
the process of receiving their degrees. Many are approaching the three year
limitation for completing th eir degree work as provided for b y our Code. lt
would behoove all Lodges through their Senior Wardens to do all that is
possible to see to it that coachin g is comple ted an<l these candidates advanced. Something prompted the m to solicit the degrees, and they shoul<l
be added to our membe rship roste r as promptly as possible. Forfeitures of
fees and con trib utions should be a rarity if these candidates receive the
encouragement and proper coaching to which t hey arc entitled to complete
their degree work.
During this past year our Membership Department has devoted <'Onsiderable time in working closely with th e Lodge Secretaries in an effort
to"purify" ou r membership listiugs. For the most part the Secretaries have

Du.Es AND Lt.FE MEMBERSHIP FEES
We are finding that an increasing number of Lodges neglect to secure
approval following adoption of an amendm ent to their By-Laws. This is

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

particularly true when the amendment concerns Lodge dues. It is mandatory that any amendment to the Uniform Code of By-Laws he approved hy
the Grand Master or his designee, and if such approval has not been obtained, the adopted amendment is not effective. In addition to this. neglect,
another area of neglect needs to be commented upon and that is Life Memberships. There are 247 Lodges in our Jurisdiction which have adopted Life
Membership Resolutions. During this past year we found that 87 of these
Lodges either never rece ived approval of their Life Me mbership Resolution ,
never received approval when the Life Membership fee was changed or
never bothered to change their Life Membership fee occasioned by a change
in their dues. This is a se rious problem since it affects the general me mbership of the Lodge and could cause trouble at a later date. Our Code
provides the formula for determining the minimum fee to be charged for
the purchase of a Life Membership, and it is suggested that when a Resolution is introduced to change the Lodge's dues and the Lodge has a Lifo
Membership plan, a companion Resolution be introduced at the same time
to change the Life Membership fee to maintain the proper ratio to the
Lodge's dues. It should also be remembered that when a Lodge votes to
rescind its Life Memhe rship Resolution, such action must be approved by
the Grand Master or his designee before such rescinding action becomes
effective.

are dedicated to doing everything in their power to enhance the image of
California Masonrv. As the members of the Executive Committee of Grand
Lodge they have -met frequently and have mutually agreed on courses of
action to he taken to solve problems which occur. It is a privilege to witness
the harmonious manner in which thev conduct their business for the bette rme nt of the Fraternity in our Jurisdiction. I would repeat what I stated
last year in my report and that is, that each of our Constituent Lodges would
do we ll to form a similar Executive Committee composed of the Master and
War dens and thus emulate on the Lodge level what is being accomplished
at the Grand Lodge level.
ln closing this Annual Report may I state that it has been an extreme

I sincerely thank them for this privilege. To serve as Grand Secretary is
indeed a most satisfying and pleasurable experience.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

TRIAL RECORD No. 2200

expelled by the Lodge on April 1, 1982, and which was affirmed by Grand
Lodge on October 12, 1982.
Among the factors taken into consideration was that the me mbers of Westminste r-Fai rview Lodge No. 327, voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement. It is the opinion of the Trial Review Committee that although the
applicant was guilty of unmasonic conduct, he· has shown substantial evidence of his atonement and rehabilitation regarding the circumstances leading to his expulsion.
The sincere desire to be restored to the rights and privileges of Mason ry
evidenced in his application leads your Committee to be lieve the applicant
has paid sufficiently for his transgressions.
Sufficient time has e lapsed since his expulsion in this case to justify restoration .
Your Committee, therefore, submits the following resolution.
RESOLVED, that the application for restoration in Trial Record No. 2177,
be approved.

In Trial Record No. 2200, the ac.-cused is a member of Meridian Lodge
No. 105 of the Grand Lodge of Montana , residing in the Coachella Valley
area of California.
In March, 1983, the accused was charged in the Municipal Court, Desert
Judicial District, Riverside County of violation of California Pe nal Code
Section 487 (1), a Fe lony (Grand Theft). The charges in the criminal case
specified that he had e mbezzled approximately $2, 100 from his e mployer
in June, 1982. It was alleged that the accused, a salesman for a steel and
supply firm , sold a welder and aceessories to a concrete company, had the
check made payable to him , cashed the check and retained the proceeds.
In the Criminal case, the accused entered into a plea of Nolo Contendere
(no contest) to a reduced charge constituting a misdemeanor and was sentenced to three years prohation and a jail term of 180 days, all but 4.5 of
which were suspended .
Since the accused is a member of a Montana Lodge, the matter was
referred to that jurisdiction. Under the impression that the accused had
bee n convicted of a f elony, the Grand Master of Montana suspended the
accused. Upon learning the accused had been convicted of a misdemeanor.
and there being no provision in the Montana Penal Code dealing with misde meanor convictions vis a vis felony convictions , the Grand Mas ter of
Montana rescinded his order of suspension and restored the accnsed to
me mbe rship.
Whereupon, a Lodge in California, exercising its jurisdiction over the
accused becanse he resides in this state, instituted a trial charging him with
unmasonic conduct under the provisions of the California Masonic Code
resulting in a findin g of not guilty on a vote of 5 to 4.
Your Committee on Trial Review carefully considered all the evidence
provided to it and concludes that the actions of the accused underlying the
proceedings in this matter are of a substantial and serious nature. The accused betrayed the confide nce and trust imposed in him by his e mployer.
But for a quirk in Montana law, he might have stood trial in his own Lodge.
Your Committee furthe r helieve s that said actions involve moral turpitude
warranting a result contrary to that of the TriaJ Maste r below, that the
verdict should be re ve rsed, a finding be made of guilt as to the charge and
specification, and the penalty fixed at expulsion.
We therefore submit the following Resolution :
RESOLVED, that the finding of the Trial Commission be reversed, a
finding be made of guilt as to the charge and specification and the penalty

of unmasonic conduct.
Once again, your Trial Review Committee finds itself in sympathy with,

reached its verdict ; we are, however, diametrically differing in our judgment and the proper result. Your Committee has repeatedly stressed that

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:

Another year has carved its path upon our Fraternity in this Grand
Jurisdiction and in compliance with those sections of our California Masonic Code. I herewith present my annual report .
In preparing this report I deem it necessary to acquaint the Brethren
with the temporary physical setback suffered by me the latter part of June.
It could not have come at a more inopportune time. While every day of
the year is relatively busy, the months of July, August and September are
very busy months for the Ritual Committee. During this period we. are
working on preparations for this Annual Meeting, regular committee
meetings, Inspectors' reports, Resolutions , questionnaires for next year's
Lodge officers, approval of expense claims. preparation of the annual
budget request. this report, information and instruction for next ye~r·s
Grand Lodge Officers, Schools of Instruction for Inspectors, the ongoing
preparation for Grand Lodge ceremonies and functions in the various
Divisions and a whole myriad of other items.
May I be permitted to express my gratitude to those seven wonderful
Assistant Grand Lecturers. They deserve my highest praise for filling
those never-ending gaps during my absence. These fine men truly played
their role of "assisting" the Grand Lecturer in the discharge of his duties
and to perform such other duties as may be required . I would be remiss
if I did not single out the efforts on my behalf by Ulysses George Patropulos for chairing the committee.
COMMITTEE MEETINGS, CONFERENCES, SEMINARS

A number of Ritual Committee meetings were held to discuss and take
action on the many inquiries placed with the Grand Lecturer and this
committee in regard to ritual, protocol and administration.
Our year has heen relatively busy and one with a sense of accompfahment. At the last Communication, you Brethren approved monotonal
changes in the first degree lecture. These changes were prepared and
printed soon thereafter and are available from the Supply Room on "G"
floor. Work was finalized relative to the printing of the latest Funeral
Ceremony book and is also available at the same location . Installation
Ceremony books were also out of print and your Ritual Committee made
the necessary review and updates previous to its printing. Ritual Committee meetings were held in conjunction with the six Annual Spring Conferences . The work of all degrees , including Masters and Candidates lectures were exemplified at each Conference as follows :
Division VI Division V

the Worshipful Morton B. Glick.

A number of Ritual seminars were held by the Assistant Grand Lecturers and Inspectors for the benefit of the Officers and Brethren throughout this Jurisdiction. These seminars were well received and attended
which indicates a great desire on the part of many to perfect their ritual
and their desire to improve the uniformity of the adopted work throughout
this Jurisdiction.
LODGES

Information disseminated from Inspectors' reports informs us that ritual
proficiency rating of Officers is reasonably good. In my last report to you
I indicated my serious concern regarding the number listed as poor. I also
said that this should not be condoned in any way. I was serious about those
remarks and am happy to report a definite improvement in this area. This
is not to say that our problems arc cured . There arc absolutely no circumstances in which ritual should be performed in this Jurisdiction by anyone
with a poor rating.
The newly adop!ed Funeral Certificate program has not been in effect
long enough to show the desired result. However, I am happy to report
that there has been significant improvement in Lodges which have np
certificate holders. Instead of 77 Lodges without a certificate holder, we
now have only 49. The overall number of certificates in our Jurisdiction
has been slightly reduced, hut I am sure we will be able to look forward
to improvements in both of these areas as soon as this program of certification and the use of the new Funeral Ceremony book becomes more
prevalent.
RITUAL

The ritual of the three degrees is near perfection at the Inspector level
of instruction , as witnessed by this Grand Lecturer at the Annual Spring
Conferences. Unfortunately, our ritual level begins to change quite dramatically in some of our Lodges, so dramatically it is not even recognizable
at times. We have a number of Lodge Officers and Inspectors in attendance at this Communication that know which Lodges I am referring to.
Brethren, we are losing candidates and our studies show a large loss after
the first degree. We also know our losses remain too high after the other
degrees. I have said it before and will say it again, that because some, and
I do wish to qualify this adverb, some of our Officers and members practice

48

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

a lackadaisical approach to the ritual of our degrees, and because of that
approach we are losing the opportunity we have been given to impress
the candidate with the dignity and high importance of our Fraternity. Too
many times the work is done in a slipshod manner. Officers are mumbling
the words because they have been poorly memorized and because they
hope that others may not recognize their mistakes. This does not work
and most certainly impresses no one. Many times, those who are appointed to fill vacancies have little or no advance preparation before filling
a place. Some of our Officers and members believe they are the greatest
ritualists in the world and need little or no practice before a degree, and
the sad fact is they can't even speak a full sentence without being
prompted. Brethren, if we arc to retain our membership, if we are to
retain our candidates, and if we are to insure our future survival , we must
put an immediate stop to the above described practices and failure on
behalf of some of our Lodges. Masters, Officers Coaches, and Inspectors,
it is your duty to see that improvements are made . Our ritual at the Lodge
level must be improved if we are to return to what this Jurisdiction once
was and can be, in the future.
HAWAIIAN MASONRY

The authority given at the last Communication to establish a new Division in this Jurisdiction has sparked a new wave of enthusiasm among
our Island Brethren. This year has been used to make Division VII function in the same manner as our other six Divisions. The format is in place
and functioning rather well under the very able direction and leadership
of Assistant Grand Lecturer Oswald J.B. Lau. While there are still a few
rough spots to work out, the accomplishment and desired result will take
place in the not too distant future.

49

individuals deserve our highest praise and respect for their limitless devotion to duty.
My thanks, on behalf of the Grand Lodge and the Ritual Committee,
to those of the corps who have chosen retirement, for their Jove of our
order and untiring efforts. It is also a distinct pleasure and honor to welcome those new Inspectors who have been appointed this year. I will be
looking forward with great enthusiasm , to working with each of you.
CONC LUSION

In concluding this report, I again pay tribute to my associates on the
Ritual Committee and to the Inspectors of the entire Jurisdiction for their
whole-hearted cooperation and their kind thoughtfulness during my recent
illness. To those Grand Lodge Officers and to all of the Brethren who.
through their good wishes and letters of encouragement, contributed so
much to my happiness and quick recovery. I wish to convey my heart-felt
thanks. To our Grand Secretary. Robert A. Klinger. and his wonderful
staff in the Grand Lodge office for their ready and able assistance. a
sincere thank you. And to you. my Brethren, my humble thanks for allowing me the opportunity to be of service to you and this great Fraternity
of ours.
Respectfully submitted.
JoE HAMMOND , Grand Lecturer
Most Worshipful, I move for the adoption of this report and that it be
referred to the Committee on Distribution.
The Committee on Distribution stated that on their perusal of this Report there was no subject matter therein making it necessary to refer it to
a Committee, so no referral was made.

BUDGET

Although costs for the continuance of instruction in ritual and administration have continued on an upward trend, I am pleased to report that
all three ritual budgets were well under those moneys allocated at the last
Annual Communication. Those who are charged with these areas of expenditure are prudent men and have kept costs within those limits prescribed by this Grand Lodge. In accordance with those procedures followed previously, formal requests have been submitted to the Finance
Committee for consideration .
INSPECTORS

The duties of the Inspector are set forth in Section 1122 of the California
Masonic Code. However, while not listed in the C.M.C. , many additional
duties and burdens have been added to their endless list of responsibilities.
With each passing year. they are asked for just a little more. Their's is an
indispensable service which is provided to our Fraternity and these 166

GRAND MASTER 'S MESSAGE

ancient and honorable institution. I thank you, each of you. for your
support as well as for your own efforts to encourage and promote Masonry's interest and for applying your God given talents to the task before us.
One year ago when I addressed this body I asked each of you to commit
yourself to assist in regaining a strong, active membership and in turning
around our downward trends. I felt we needed a brave new strategy to
improve participation , strengthen communicat ion and increase membership. Together, the members of your Executive Committee established
these goals and we announced the following objectives in the Winter issue
of the California Freemason:
First , officer developmen t by helping incumbent and prospective Lodge
officers become more proficient in planning, organizing and implementin g
their Lodge programs. Provide Lodge managemen t training programs and
workshops to help all Masonic Leaders become more effective in the performance of their responsibilit ies.
Next, Lodge programmin g by developing helpful programs and resources to provide Lodge leaders with ideas and formats for interesting
programs; programs that can help improve participation and attract members (and prospective members) to become involved .
Third , Masonic responsibilit y by emphasizing the need for an understanding of Masonry, not only by the candidates for the degrees , but also
for the benefit of long time Masons. Masonic responsibilit y includes improving our personal Masonic knowledge as well as recognizing our obligations to relieve our distressed worthy Brothers, and their dependents.
And, finally, social respo nsibility and recognizing our role in the community. Reemphasiz ing total involvement in those programs that extend
outside the Lodge rooms.
Those arc long-term objectives based upon our evaluation of the
strengths and weaknesses of our Jurisdiction . I realize. as you should, that
we cannot expect results to occur overnight. Therefore many of our actions
this past year have been aimed at long-term improvemen ts rather than
short-term " first aid" treatments.
My Brethren, we need a high profile Freemasonry . The future will not
take care of itself. It is in our hands. We must continue to take the steps
necessary to help people understand who we are , what we do. why we do
it and how people benefit therefrom ; and Brethren , those who must understand Masonry include not only persons not familiar with our Fraternity, but also our own members and their families. Yes. our own Brethren
must become knowledgea ble. Our own Brethren must become concerned.
Our own Brethren must open the ir eyes. Our own Brethren need a renewed spirit.

The first action taken this year was to introduce the Fraternal Management Course. We are indebted to Bill Jones, managemen t expert, with

STRENGTHEN TRADITIONAL VALUES
Our ne xt goal is to STRENGTHEN TRADITIONAL VALUES
WITHIN THE LODGE SYSTEM. When we objectively review our
strengths and weaknesses as an organization , I believe it is clear that our
basic strength results from Masonry's age-old Lodge structure and our
freely-given individual co mmitment to our traditional values.
"Our ~reatest need is for an increased knowledge among Master Masons
of the history and fundamentals of Freemasonry and an earnest striving
to use these fundamentals inside the Lodge as well as outside." These
~or?s by Past Grand Master Gene Hopp over 15 years ago echo the
ftndmgs of the Special Commission in 1963 which reported the consensus
of those polled that our number one problem then was lack of teaching
of Masonic fundamentals.
But, you say, that's the purpose of our ritual. Nothing could be further
from the truth. The ritual is important , but " after conferring of the degrees
... too many of our Lodges consider their responsibilitv of informing the
candidates about Masonry to be at an end," so concluded Past Grand
Master Chet MacPhee in 1970. Consequently, the Masonic Information
and Responsibility Committee was established to help develop methods
to improve our Masonic knowledge , and at the same time encourage, if

G RAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

not assure , participation. Participation and effective Lodge management
are the keys to a Lodge's future. You officers must apply your God-given

Proper handling of new members requires greater emphasis. Equally
important to gaining new members is their prope r orientation, investigation and coaching. In recent years nearly 20% of those initiated as an
Entered Apprentice have not continued on to the Master Mason Degree.
20 years ago this number was less than 2%. We've asked the Masonic
Information and Responsibility Committee to hold seminars throughout
the Jurisdiction with Lodge candidate coaches. We must encourage and
help the coaches to provide the candidates with understanding and explanations of the Masonic symbolism in addition to the teaching of the words
necessary for passing a proficiency. The unsung heroes of our Lodges too
often are .the candidate coaches. We've asked the Committee to explore
ways to give these coaches proper recognition, and I would hope such a
means will be forthcoming soon. I'm disappointed it hasn't already occurred.
Don't forget that all important and very effective. "Lodge System of
Masonic Information For Candidates" with the excellent booklet for use
by your Lodge's committee. Table discussions such as proposed by that

What do you think? Is it time to reassess this custom ?

The consequences of this decision are significant. All California Masons
residing in New Jersey are affected as are members of New Jersey Lodges
residing in this Jurisdiction. Your Lodges are admonished not to accept
them as regular Masons and you are to have no fraternal relations with a
Mason carrying a New Jersey dues card , including meetings held by those
organizations concordant to or subject to the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of the State of California, including but not limited to the Scottish
Rite, York Rite, Eastern Star and Order of Amaranth .
The alternative to your concurring with my decision would be to amend
our law, specifically C.M.C. Section 2622 as at least one other jurisdiction
has done , to make it possible for a resident of this Jurisdiction to apply
to a Lodge in any jurisdiction without first obtaining a Waiver of Jurisdiction. However, such a change would, in my opinion, be to the detriment
of our Fraternity in general and this Jurisdiction in particular and would
serve no useful purpose.

Each Grand Master has the responsibility to make recommendations
and decisions which he thinks may be helpful or are necessary for the
welfare of the Craft. Many of these recommendations and decisions lead
to change in our pattern which tend to strengthen us, but the determination concerning these is in the hands of you, the Grand Lodge. I urge
that each of you give thoughtful consideration to these recommendations
and decisions for the good of this Jurisdiction and its future.

Decision Number I
Prior to the last Annual Communication Grand Master Harry L. Maynard directed the Ritual Committee to prepare and present a "Table Lodge
Ceremony" and to present some guidelines for such a program.
Misunderstanding apparently exists relative to the use of this Ceremony.
To clear up any misunderstanding, it is my Decision that the "Table Lodge
of Fellowship Ceremony" previously developed by the Ritual Committee
of this Grand Lodge be recognized as a "social event" for the Constituent
Lodges for the purpose of promoting fraternal fellowship and accordingly
is available for those Lodges interested in using it.

Decision Number 2
The Grand Lodge of California formally withdrew recognition from the
Grand Lodge of New Jersey effective August 29, 1984. The basis for this
decision is that the Grand Master of New Jersey has made it quite evident
that the Grand Lodge of New Jersey does not intend to abide by, nor
recognize the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Grand Lodge of
California; nor does it recognize the laws adopted as part of the California
Masonic Code. Specifically I refer to C.M.C., Section 2622-2 which sets
forth the procedures for a resident of this Jurisdiction to receive the Degrees of Masonry outside of the jurisdictional boundaries of this Grand
Lodge by first obtaining a Waiver of Jurisdiction.
You should all be aware of the circumstances in connection with the
ma king a Mason in New Jersey of Mr. Amos Jacobs, aka Danny Thomas,
the entertainer.
The Grand Master of New Jersey contacted me by telephone advising
me of his intent to confer the Degrees on Mr. Thomas and questioned my
position. He was advised of our regulations and our strong objections in
the absence of a Waiver of Jurisdiction being requested. It was the decision
of the Grand Master of New Jeresey to confer the Degrees in that State
without the required Waiver of Jurisdiction on the basis that Mr. Thomas
was a "citizen of the world''. Futile attempts were made over many months
to bring about a reconciliation with New Jersey, but without cooperation
on their part we were unable to do so.
Under our C.M.C. Section 2682, Mr. Jacobs (Thomas) could not be
recognized as a Mason in California nor could we contact him under our

RECOMMENDATIONS
Our ritual for each of the three Degrees requires that the candidate
commit to memoi:.y a portion of the lecture, the Obligation and the answer
to certain questions, to enable the candidate to pass a satisfactory proficiency prior to the conferral of the next Degree. Further, Section 2635 of
the California Masonic Code states that to apply for membership in a
prerequisite organization , a Mason must "have given satisfactory evidence ,
by strict examination in open Lodge, that he is proficient and qua lified in
the Candidates' Lecture of the Degree of Master Mason and not until
after the lapse of one year from the date he receives the Degree of Master
Mason ."
I have considered our problems of membership and the fact that about
18% of all who are initiated fail to become Master Masons . This past yea r
378 candidates forfeited their fee and contributions rather than continue
on and complete their degree work. I have searched for causes. I have
evaluated recommendations given me. I have inquired of actions taken by
other jurisdictions and evaluated their comparative results. From this combined evaluation , I recommend the following:

Second and Third Degrees which will carry out the intent of this Rec-

Page 33 of the Installation Service for Constituent Lodges includes the
instruction, "Photographs should not be taken while the service is in progress." The intent of this instruction is to insure that nothing disrupts the
dignity and attention given to the ceremony. However, with fast film and
VCR cameras, flash and floods are no longer necessary. I see nothing
harmful in recording, by picture or sound, the ceremony for the future
pleasure of the officer being installed.
I recommend that approval for the use of cameras and/or audio equipment be at the discretion of the installing officer. Should this approval be
given , the persons performing the recording, and all persons attending,
should be cautioned not to use flash or flood lamps and not to move around
the room or in any way disrupt the solemnity of the ceremony.

Recommendation No. 2

These self-imposed rules are , in my opinion, standing in the way of our
progress and growth without providing any real benefit. Certainly, we gain
nothing in participation when only 5% of our members other than Officers, attend Degrees and only 6.5% attend Stated Meetings. Certainly we
haven't helped our membership statistics, which continue downward at an
alarming rate, and it is often reported that men otherwise interested in
petitioning for Degrees are discouraged from doing so because of the
commitment of time to memorize the ritual of our proficiency requirement. Certainly we are not helping the Mason who is interested in serving
Masonry in one of the concordant or affiliated groups requiring Masonic
membership nor are we helping those organizations and their membership
concerns which are not unlike our Lodges. Certainly we haven't helped
those who have been initiated because in recent years , about 18% of those
Entered Apprentice Masons have failed to be Passed and Raised. I am
convinced that those passing the Proficiency do not necessarily understand
our Masonic principles any better than those from other jurisdictions not
requiring memorization, or a very minimum of memorization such as Kansas and Pennsylvania.
Now I can understand the thinking of many of you sitting here today.
"I've done it, why can't everybody? " Well , my Brethren , the vast majority
of our members, and potential members, are not committed to the same
level of involvement as you Lodge Officers and Past Masters, and you
know it. Isn't it time we seriously review such rules and decisions? These
are not Landmarks. They are based on decisions. These are not customs
passed to us from time immemorial. They are ritualistic demands placed
on us by predecessors early in this century. In this modern age of computers, learning techniques have changed. Educators no longer consider
memorization as an effective means of understanding and learning. Let
us join the 20th Century.

CONCLUSION
And so, my Brethren, this Masonic year is nearly over. I have travel~d
over 33,000 miles by air, 18,000 by car and 1,200 by bus, addressing more
than 24,000 Masons and 36,000 of their families , friends and youth. Thank
you for your support and for your friendship and for the many courtesies
extended to my wife and me and the other Grand Lodge Officers and
their wives. I thank you for granting me the honor to serve you. I have
enjoyed the fellowship and the challenge. Many new friendships have
resulted and the experience has contributed a fullness to my life which
otherwise could never have been achieved.
I have tried my best to re-kindle a sense of enthusiastic pride in our
Fraternity. I have tried to arouse a sense of urgency to recognize the
seriousness of the downward membership and participation trends , accompanied by the apathy of the membership , so obvious throughout our Jurisdiction. I have tried to promote a high profile Freemasonry along with
a revival of the Masonic spirit we so desperately need. Only you can
determine my success. Only through your actions will my efforts be successful because quality and excellence in your Lodge operation are the
keys to Masonry's future. It is in your hands.
To my successor, I wish the very best in his year and commit my efforts
in any way I can to assist him. We have planned and worked together.
Our goals and dreams for this Grand Lodge are as one. May you enjoy

the experience and cooperation from those who arc so vitally interested
and concerned with strengthening of our Jurisdiction.
To you, my Brethren, remember, One Mason Can Make A Difference.
YOU! May the Great Architect of the Universe grant that each of you
may dedicate and devote your life to His service and be a true and faithful
Brother among us. Convince the world that on becoming a Master Mason,
you have become a better man. As members of this, the world's oldest
and largest fraternal organization. let us be shy no longer. Let us go to
our strengths. the basic tenets of our honorable institution . Brotherly
Love , Relief and Truth . Let us practice what we teach. How can we not
believe in the goodness and greatness of our Fraternity!
Brethren , we need a high profile Freemasonry. Let us tell the world
who we are, what we do, why we do it and how people benefit therefrom.
Let us raise our sights. Don' t accept mediocrity. Don't be complacent.
Don't take things for granted. Time doesn't change things; leaders change
things. I challenge you to accept your responsibilities as Masonic leaders.
How can we not do our best to instill in our membership a renewed pride,
enthusiasm and commitment. Let us have a revival of the Masonic spirit.
Freemasonry must never be stagnant; it must always be advancing.
Above all, my Brethren , remember your obligations, freely given on
the volume of the Sacred Law. A strict adherence to those words; can we
ask less of a Mason? Freemasonry is an individual matter. an individual
responsibility and an individual opportunity. Apply the teachings of Freemasonry every day to your life and you will be adding to our great heritage. Remember also the words of the Master when he admonished you
to wear the lambskin apron with pleasure to yourself and honor to the
Fraternity. Pleasure to yourself and honor to the Fraternity. Yes, My
Brethren . let us be serious about our Fraternity; but let us also never
forget to enjoy our experiences.
One Mason Can Make A Difference-YOU!
Thank you.

DECISION No. 1

TABLE LODGE CEREMONY

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Decision No. l of the Most
Worshipful Grand Master has been submitted, reports as follows:
The Grand Master has now decided to clear up any misunderstandings.
that th~ "Table Lodge of Fellowship'' be recognized as a "social event"
for the Constituent Lodges, for the purpose of promoting fellowship.
This Decision is well adapted to its purpose.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, your Committee moves
that the Decision be approved.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Last year the Grand Lodge rejected a recommendation that a particular
Tahle Lodge for Fellowship Ceremony drafted by the Ritual Committee
be adopted as the only ceremony for use by Lodges which desired the
Table Lodge for Fellowship as a social event.
Decision Number One purports to clarify matters so that any Lodge
may use any Table Lodge for Fellowship format it desires to use, thus
correcting any impression that the Table Lodge concept had been disapproved.
This means that Grand Lodge, if it adopts this Decision , would be
reversing last year's action and allowing use of only one ceremony, to wit.
that created by !<he Ritual Committee.
This, in effect , means that the Grand Lodge is mandating a social event.
We reiterate our statements of last year:
"Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that
Grand Lodge should control the acts of the Constituent Lodges
as to ritual, accounting, etc. However, we are concerned that
the adoption of the formal Table Lodge Ceremony moves into
the realm of controlling the social programs of a Lodge. Your
Committee can foresee the time when possibly a ritual and
scenerio for a Widow's Pin Ceremony or Layman's Night would
be mandated.
"Therefore , your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
believes that as a guideline for those Lodges desiring to participate in a Table Lodge Ceremony, the proposed ceremony will
accomplish the intent and can be printed without approval of
Grand Lodge. However. your Committee is concerned that
such a fellowship program not become an edict of this Grand
Lodge and therefore we recommend a 'No' vote."

The Committee on Ritual:
The Committee on Ritual concurred with the Decision of the Grand
Master and recommended a "Yes" vote.

Our research discloses that the American Doctrine (sometimes called
"Territorial exclusiveness") is defined by H enry Wilson Coil in his highly
respected " Masonic Encyclopedia" published in 1961 , to mandate that
there can be but one Grand Lodge in an American state , and that such
Grand Lodge must have exclusive Masonic jurisdiction within its territorial borders.
The Doctrine, we find, had its origin in this country while independent
G rand Lodges were being formed both during a nd following the American
Revolution. It is true that for nearly one hundred years, there were reported violations of the Doctrine in isolated cases; however, by the end
of the 19th century, the American Doctrine of territorial exclusiveness was
universally acce pted , in this countr y.
You will discover refe rence to the adhe rence by this Grand Lodge to
the American Doctrine as far back as 1859 in the G rand Master's Message
to the Craft delivered by Most Worshipful N. C urtis Greene . Grand Master Jonathan Doan Hines concluded in 1884 that it would not be proper
for a Lodge in California to receive and act upon an application from a
citizen of another state because ... "(It) involves the same principle exercised by our Grand Lodge in de nying to pe rsons residing in this State
the right to petition for and receive the degrees in anothe r jurisdiction ."
More recently, in 1948, then Grand Master, Most Worshipful Edward
H . Siems, recognized and refe rred to the Doctrine in dealing with a breach
by a sister jurisdiction.
T he doctrine is well established in America and serves an essential
Masonic purpose . Section 7b of our Califo rnia Masonic Code states in
part . .. "{This) Grand Lodge adhe res to the American Doctrine of exclusive territo rial jurisdiction ...". Again in Section IOOd.2. of our law
we find: " Any G1and Body seeking recognition as a sovereign Grand
Lodge (i n English speaking countries) ... must . .. recognize the excl usive jurisdiction of all othe r Grand Lodges in their respective territories,
and must not presume to project its authority or sovereignty into the
territory of any other Grand Lodge ."
The authority of Grand Maste r H aglund to sever fraternal relations with
the Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of New Jersey is without question. Li kewise,
his authority to forbid California Masons to attend Masonic Lodges in
New Jersey is well established by Section 241 2 of the C. M.C., as that
section requires a Master Mason before visiting anot her Lodge to satisfy
himself of its lawful authority.
Furthermore, to the extent that the Grand Master directed Lodges in
this Jurisdiction to forbid admittance to Masons who ho ld membership
solely in a Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of New Jersey,
his executive power to do so is confirmed by Section 2416 of the California
Masonic Code.
Finally, altho ugh the Gra nd Master does not speak directly to the issue
in his Decision No. 2, we believe that by way of clarification , it should be

DEc1s10N No. 2
WITHDRAWAL OF RECOGNITION FROM
GRAND LODGE OF NEW JE RS E Y

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Yo ur Committee on Jurisprudence , to which G rand Master's Decision
No. 2 was referred, reports as follows:
In order to evaluate the propriety of Grand Master Haglund's decision
to withdraw the frate rnal recognition of the Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of
New Jersey by this Grand Lodge, and of his edicts affecting fraternal
intercourse between the Brethren of the two jurisdictions, we have examined not only his Decision, but , also, the lette rs of communication
between the two Grand Masters , memoranda recorded by o ur Grand Master, and his letters to the constituent Lodges of o ur Jurisdiction .
In conducting this investigation . we note that G rand Maste r Haglund's
forbearance has been admirable and in historic Masonic tradition under
most distressing circumstances, and we have concluded that his action in
withdrawing recognition of the fraternally offending siste r jurisdiction was
entirely correct and mandated by our law.
The facts leading to the Grand Master's Decision, briefly stated, are:
1. A resident of the State of California petitioned a Lodge under the

jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of New Je rsey, to receive the degrees
of Masonry.
2. The then G rand Master of New Jersey, apparently recognizing the
well established American Doctrine which grants exclusive jurisdiction of Grand Lodges over residents in the ir respective territories,
asked our Grand Master by telephone whether o ur G rand Lodge
would object to a resident of California receiving the degrees o f
Masonry in New Je rsey.
3. Grand Master Haglund informed the New J ersey Gra nd Master that
there would be no objection if a Lodge near the residence of the
Applicant waived its jurisdiction over him.
4. The New Jersey G rand Maste r, acting on behalf of his Gra nd Lodge ,
rejected our Grand Maste r's dete rmination , and proceeded to allow
the degrees of Masonry to be conferred upon the applica nt (an entertainer) through some process of determining that he was not exclusively a resident of California but, rather. "a citizen of the wo rld."
5. Many months e lapsed during which Grand Master Haglund , Gra nd
Secretary Klinger. and many others sought in the most gentle traditions of our Bro therhood , to seek a resolution. Their e ffo rts we re
in vai n .

75

76

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

California. is entitled unde r C.M.C. Section 2032c to seek fraternal intercourse with the Lodges and the Brethren under the jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge of California.
This interpretation, simply stated, requires only that a Mason be a member of at least one recognized jurisdiction whether or not he holds dual
membership in a jurisdiction that is not recognized. It follows. of course.
that a California jurisdiction Mason who holds dual membership in a New
Jersey Lodge , or any other unrecognized Lodge is permitted to attend
Lodges in this jurisdiction and to retain fraternal relations with his Brethren in this and any other jurisdiction recognized by the Grand Lodge of
California. This is because he is a member of a Lodge in a jurisdiction
recognized by California ; to wit, its own Lodge.
The Grand Master's Decision conforms to this opinion; it properly expresses our law; and 'we move its approval.

The Committee on Policy and Ge,;eral Purposes:
When the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of New Jersey persisted
in ignoring the American Doctrine of exclusive territorial jurisdictio n.
despite attempts by our Grand Master to reconcile the problem , as o ur
Grand Master described in his Message to this Grand Lodge, he had no
recourse but to withdraw recognition of the Grand Lodge of New Jersey.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends approval
of that decision by this Grand Lodge.
However, as a result of the withdrawal of recognition there is an immediate consequence upon the Masons of New Jersey residing in California, and upon Masons holding dual memhership in California and New
Jersey Lodges. A similar consequence descends upon California Masons
residing in New Jersey.
The consequence of withdrawal of recognition is that no Masonic communication can be held between the "regular" Masons of California and
the unrecognized or "irregular" Masons of New Jersey. This ban on communication would extend to prerequisite bodies whose membership is dependent upon membership in a Lodge of a jurisdiction formally recognized
by our Grand Lodge .
Those holding dual membership in Lodges of both Grand Lodges involved find themselves in a particularly disturbing situation.
In order to maintain a proper Masonic intercourse with the California
Lodge , the dual members were required, by direction of our Grand Master, to request a dimit from their New Jersey Lodges. Failure to present
proof of a request for dimit would result in an immediate bar to communication with the California constituent Lodge in which they hold dual
membership.
Your Committee can foresee some unusual problems arising from this
requirement.
For example, it can be presumed that eventual reconciliation between
the Grand Lodges will be effected. What then becomes of the memberships in New Jersey for which prompt <limits were required? Will these

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

77

members reinstate their New Jersey membership through re-application?
It is doubtful that many such former members would re-apply.
Therefore, the acts of the intransigent Grand Master of New Jersey,
who refused to conform to recognized Masonic authority, would create an
undue burden on members and Lodges in his jurisdiction and ours in spite
of eventual reconciliation.
In addition , what becomes of California members now residing or visiting in New Jersey and who are unaware of the withdrawal of recognition?
Do they become •·tainted"' if they visit Lodges in New Jersey and thereby
become so contaminated they cannot continue or resume Masonic communication with their California Brethren?
The questions raised here bear further consideration by this Grand
Lodge. A possible solution might be to provide a "cooling off" period in
such situations, a period not explicitly provided for in present California
law.
Therefore . your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends that the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee to
study the consequences to our members at withdrawal of recognition of
another jurisdiction. with a view to presenting legislation to this Grand
Lodge to prevent undue hardship to our members.
We recommend approval of Grand Master's Decision Number 2.
The Grand Master's Decision was approved.

Hear the word of Edwin Markham:
"We are all blind until we see, that in the human plan,
Nothing is worth the making, if it does not make the man.
Why build these cities glorious, if man unbuilded goes,
In vain we build the building, unless the builder also grows."
My Brethren , what purpose the structure of Freemasonry if we do not
continue to build Freemasons?
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No"
vote.

the Recommendation.

The Committee on Ritual:

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Only the Grand Lodge has the authority to change ritual. Your Grand
Lecturer stands willing and able to make those changes providing this
Recommendation is adopted.

The Grand Master has proposed, in Recommendation No. 1, that the
requirements for advancement in the Degrees be reduced to memorizing
the several obligations and the modes of recognition, thus , eliminating the
necessity of reciting the ''Candidates Lectures" as we now know them.
In recent years a substantial number of candidates have failed to advance to the sublime Degree of Master Mason , resulting in the forfeiture
of all fees and rights of participation. Based upon the statistics and pe rcentages it is readily convenient to indict the ritualistic requirements as
the probable cause. Your Committee on Policy an<l General Purposes does
not believe there is sufficient evidence , if any, to support this theory. The
true reasons for failure to complete the Degree work can only be determined from the Candi<lates themselves and that information is not available to us.
We believe that for every Candidate who may be discouraged or disillusioned by our requirements there are hundreds of members whose values
of Freemasonry are strengthened and solidified by the commitment of
dedication expected from them in "earning" the right to become a complete member of this ancient craft.
While it is true that in this modern age of computers learning techniques
have changed , it is also true that nothing designed or created by man has
replaced the God-given gift of a keen mind because of its ability to learn
from rather than just retain information. As each of you registered for
this Communication you received a pamphlet, produced by the Grand
Lodge of California, entitled, " Freemasonry-A Way of Life ." It is beautifully done and in the centerfold you will find these words regarding
learning: " Even men in their later years often surprise themselves. Anything worthwhile deserves an honest effort, and reasonable effort can
·
produce success." .
The Masons of today, you and I, have had entrusted to our care the
ritualistic lessons that have been handed down from "mouth to ear" from
generation to generation. Who among you will preserve the integrity of
the ritual if it is not required? Who among you will be able to transmit
the unblemished lessons of the nineteen eighties to the generations of the
two thousands?

RECOMMENDATION No. 3

PROFICIENCY FOR CONCORDANT
AND APPENDANT BODIES

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Recommendation No. 3
of the Most Worshjpful Grand Master has been referred, reports as follows:
The Grand Master proposes to modify our law so as to permit a Master
Mason who has failed to qualify in the Candidate's Lectures within five
years of the date that he was raised to the Master Mason degree to apply,
after said period, for membership in concordant bodies.
To carry out the Grand Master's intent , your Committee submits the
following legislation:
RESOLVED, that Section 2635 of the California Masonic Code be
amended to read :
"A Mason who applies and is elected to receive the degrees of
Masonry in a Lodge of this Jurisdiction shall not apply for nor
receive any degree or be initiated into any organization , other
than another Lodge, the prequisite of membership wherein is
that a person be a Mason, until he has given satisfactory evidence, by strict examination in open Lodge , that he is proficient and qualified in the Candidate's Lecture of the Degree of
Master Mason and until the lapse of one year from the date he
received the Degree of Master Mason; provided, however, that
each such Master Mason shall be free of this restriction five
years following the date that he received the said Master Mason

80

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

degree . The restriction referred to herein does not apply to
organizations which do not confer degrees and do not have
form al initiation ceremonies."
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge , we move the adoption of
the Resolution .

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Haglund's Recommendation No. 3 concerns Section 2635
of the California Masonic Code entitled "Membership in Prerequisite Organizations."
Since October 1953, a Mason who applied and was elected to receive
the degrees of Masonry in a Lodge of this Jurisdiction first was required
to give satisfactory evidence, by strict examination in open Lodge, that
he was proficient and qualified in the Candidate's Lecture of the Degree
of Master Mason , before he was able to apply and be elected to a Concordant Masonic body; and then only and until after the lapse of one year
from the date he rece ived the Degree of Master Mason.
The Grand Master's Recommendation No. 3 would limit the foregoing
requirement to a period of time not to exceed five years from the date on
which the Candidate received the Degree of Master Mason.
As the foregoing proficie ncy requirement did not exist prior to October
1953, when it was first adopted , this Recommendation of the Grand Master would make our law in this regard the same as it was originally; for
this Recommendation seeks to allow the Masons, who for a period of five
years after receiving the Degree of Master Mason have not complied with
Section 2635 of the California Masonic Code, to petition and be elected
to a prerequisite Masonic body without restrictio n by our Grand Lodge.
Many of our Brethren for reasons of their own have failed to comply
with our present law; and if after five years from the date they received
the Third Degree of Freemasonry they have not passed the present required proficiency in that Degree, your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes believes that the y should no longe r be restricted from seeking
further light in Masonry in a Concordant Body if they wish to do so,
without the present re quirement as set o ut in the aforementioned Section
2635.
We, the refore, recommend a "Yes" vote on Grand Master's Recommendation No. 3.

The Committee on Ritual:
Legislation on this subject has been too long in coming. Your Committee on Ritual is in complete concurrence and recommends a " Yes" vote.
Failing a 516 affirmative vote but receiving a ma jority favorable vote ,
the Grand Maste r's Recommendation No. 3 is held over until the 1985
Communication.

PROCLAMATION
MASONIC AWARENESS WEEK
Masons are proud of their heri tage and the fact that they are members
of the oldest and mo st respected fraternal organi~ation known t o man, having for
its foundation th e practice of the social a nd moral vi rtues. If each Mason exhibits the pri de that he feels for his Fraternity, there will result a reviva l
of the Masonic spirit so necessary throughout our membership.
Masons should ever bear in mind that exclusively in those areas of the
world where freedom exists does Freemasonry flourish - - a fact to be proudly
shared with those who are not privileged to be counted among us. Freedom antl
Freemasonry are inseparable as Masons are enjoined to disc harge civic duties,
obey the law and give unqualified allegiance to their Country.
In every age and country, mrn preeminent for the ir moral and intellectual attainments have encouraged and 1· r'lmoted Freemasonry's interest.

In recognition of the pride we feel in and for our Masonic Fraternity
and to r emind ea ch individual Mason, his family and f r iends of the importance of
his membership in o ur F ra t er nity, I Proc l aim the week beginning Oc t ober 8, 1084
to be

MASONIC AWARENESS WEEK
in t he States of Cal iforni a and Hawaii this being the week of the 135th Annual
Comm uni~a ti on of the Grand Lodge of California.

To promote this awareness, I request that each Mason proudly Year hi s
Masonic Sq uare and Compass pin, as a means of identifyinR himself as a Freemason .
l fu rt he r encourage every Hasan to promote the interest o f o ur ancien t
and honorable institution by reconfirming his acce ptance of the burdens and responsibilities to our Fraternity as well as publicly extolling the benefits and
privileges gained th rough his Masonic experiences.
Please bring this Proclamation to the attention of all the members of
your Lodge and remi nd each that "One Mason Can Ma ke A Difference -- YOU!"
Fraternally,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, a charitable
corporation organized under the laws of the State of California , respectfully presents its ninety-second annual report on the Masonic Homes of
California for the fiscal year July 1, 1983 through June 30, 1984.

Code , they were elected members of the Board. In addition to the Grand

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

MEETINGS
The Board of Trustees meet on a monthly basis at the Masonic Homes,
alternating between the North and the South. Meeting at the Homes provides a closer look at and better understanding of the operations of each
Home.
This is a working Board dedicated to providing the facilities, staff and
environment essential to the security and happiness of our elderly at Union
City and to the health, education and development of our children at
Covina.
Many hours are spent in Committee meetings on rehabilitation, long
range planning, scholarship grants, special projects, budget and finance.
Trustees and Administrators present special reports on operations of the
Homes, resulting in a broader understanding of these complex units and
improved guidance ana management of the Homes.
