UNION CITY STATISTICS, by J. Burton Brown, Administrator
The Personal Care section has been increased from 108 residents to a
new capacity of 124 persons causing a decrease in the number of rooms
available in the Residential Living Section to 142, down from 158, but
there is no change in the total capacity of 433. The monthly average number of residents increased to 366 which included 133 men and 233 women.
Thirty-nine men with an average age of 82.9 and thirty-nine women
with an average age of 80.5 entered the Home during this fiscal year.
During the same period, twenty-one Brothers and twenty-nine of our ladies passed on to a life greater than this earthly one. The average ages
and len~h of residency for the men was 87.7 years and 4 years, 1 month;
and age 87 with 7 years, 11 months for the women.
Three of the deceased women had the distinction of living at the Home
for more than twenty-two years (one for 22, one for 23, and one for 25).
Also the two oldest residents expired within two weeks of each other;
Cora Wood age 104 and Sammuel Keiser, age 103, she after living at the
Home for seventeen years and he for eleven and a half years.
The fiscal year ended showing our total population of 374, comprised
of 137 men and 237 women. The numbers in our different levels of care
at the end of the year were as follow: Residential Living 128, Personal
Care 109, and Skilled Nursing Facility 131.
UNION CITY OPERATIONS, by J. Burton Brown, Administrator
We continue to have a waiting period of several months for approved
applicants who are married. Individual applicants are able to be accom-

UNION CITY-SPECIAL PROJECTS,
by J. Burton Brown, Administrator
Some of our special projects and potential improvements of last year
have become reality; all of which add to the comfort and services for the
residents directly or indirectly. A computerized energy management system has been installed that adds automation to most of the controls for
lights, equipment, boilers, elevators, and air conditioning. Installation of
our own television system was completed and immediately named H.E.N.
for Home Entertainment Network. We are now able to broadcast live
spiritual programs and all events in/from our auditorium to residents'
rooms in all sections of the facility. We can record desirable programs on
video tape for repeat performances, plus being able to televise a different
movie each week. In addition, we tape instructional programs and meetings for use with the employees.
Mechanical devices are not the only improvements added this year; a
large outside area near the front of the buildings has been nicely landscaped and arranged with all the equipment necessary for a barbeque and
picnics. We anticipate this area will be used by our residents, employees,
and visiting groups.
Projects that are in the planning stages include physical therapy equipment, a shuffle board court, and additional space for activities in the
skilled Nursing Facility.
COVINA OPERATIONS, by John A. Rose, Administrator
Masonry's best kept secret is indeed rapidly unfolding. The population
of our Children's Home continues to grow. At this writing we have 58
children in our Home. We have served 66 children this past fiscal year,
and several have graduated or were fortunate to be able to return to their
families. There continues to be evidence of ever-increasing numbers of
children in need.
The average number of children at our Home has increased 66% in
three years, and 87% when comparing actual numbers between fiscal years
1980/1 and 1983/4. This increase is directly attributed to improved communication regarding our Home and who may be served. It can also be
attributed to the improved level of service. The Fraternity is quickly learn-

ADMISSION TO HOMES, by John M. Palmer, Jr.,
Chairman Admissions Committee, South
To provide for maximum efficiency in Board operations, the Admission
Committee was established to review all applications prior to each Board
meeting. Since the Trustees meet alternately each month in the North and
South, the Committee has Co-chairmen, Ralph M. Hinds from the North
and John M. Palmer, Jr. from the South. Two other Trustees from the
North and two from the South complete the Committee assignments.
During the past two years an increasing number of applications for
admission to Union City have been submitted to the Board for consideration generating a population approaching the capacity of the facility. This
influx of applications has created a waiting list of some length which has
prompted a review of our approval procedures. In the past, applicants
were admitted to Union City based on their Board approval date resulting
in some inequities wherein the admittee was not necessarily the one in
most need on the waiting list.
A new concept has been approved by the Board and is being implemented by the Admissions Committee, which will admit to Union City all
of those who meet the eligibility requirements of the California Masonic
Code and its supplements. A point rating system will be used to rank the
applicants in each of three levels of care - Residential, Personal Care, and
Skilled Nursing. As openings become available in each of the care categories, the applicant on the waiting list with the greatest need will be
admitted first. Each applicant on the waiting list will be reviewed by the
Board periodically to assu~e that the status rating is still valid.

This year people traveled to California from all parts of the world to
participate and witness the Olympics. Some Californians traveled to all
parts of the world, and it is said that Southern Californians left the Los
Angeles area to avoid the expected crowds. One p!ace most of them
missed was Union City. The Masonic Home didn't have an Olympic Spectacular nor were there record crowds visiting our city, but those visitors
who came to the Home and the events which took place during this year
were as important and meaningful as the Olympics. Married couples celebrating more than 65 years of married life, several birthdays of people
over 100 years, a new High Twelve Club, and two marriages are but a few
of the historic events which took place at your Masonic Home for Adults. '
Statistics cannot adequately describe the significance of many of the
activities, but they do assist in knowing to what extent our Masonic family
participates in the life of the Home. 1\venty-six groups (Lodges, Masonic
Clubs, Widows groups, etc.) arranged to have tours of the Home; fortyfour different groups provided a wide variety of entertainment at the
Home ranging from Shrine Bands and singing groups to a 100 piece High
School Band from Utah. Groups of residents made thirty-eight trips to
various activities away from the Home (including Baseball games, concerts, plays, the opera and sightseeing trips). Here at the Home throughout the year thirty-two Bethels of Job's Daughters shared in our church
services; eleven meetings of Eastern Star Chapters were held; and all three
types of degrees were conferred upon candidates by fourteen Lodges. On
September 28, 1983 with the Deputy Grand Master in attendance, High
1\velve State President Lee Krikava chartered the Masonic Home High
1\velve Club No. 606 with 35 members, most of whom are residents of
the Home. Other State and regional officers plus wives and friends applauded a full line of Club officers as they were installed.
Historically significant is the fact that the two oldest residents died
within two weeks of each other as reported elsewhere, so Margaret Peterson of Le Progres de L'Oceanie Lodge No. 371 is our Senior Citizen
at age 102 on the 1st of July. She is joined in the over 100 group by Nona
.Hambly, Park Crockett Lodge No. 139. Special recognition is given to
those couples with anniversaries marking 65 or more years. Mr. and Mrs.
Melville Wagner celebrated their 73rd wedding anniversary on August
11th, Mr. and Mrs. Allen Cherry were next with 68 years; Mr. and Mrs.
Oarence Snygg and Mr. and Mrs. Joe Buzolich observed their 66th, and
it was number 64 for Mr. and Mrs. Albert Mattson.
Other milestones of importance centered around two employees who
chose to retire this year. Mrs. Sophie Barker, who started working at the
Home on January 1, 1949 and provided loving care to the residents for 35
years, left in June as a Certified Nursing assistant. And Eleanor Farris
started her retirement on May 31 after serving more than 23 years as our

Director of Nursing and since 1976 as the Director of Health Services.
The reputation for the high quality of care that the Home has maintained
can definitely be attributed to the dedicated leadership of Mrs. Farris and
the devotion shown to our residents by employees such as Mrs. Barker.
We will miss them and we offer our gratitude and congratulations for their
many years of service.
Traditional events continue to be a very important part of life at Masonic
Home. The Grand Master's Reception in April was enjoyed by all those
in attendance and for the first time, those residents who could not attend
were able to be a part of it. Due to the installation of our own closed
circuit television system, we transmitted all of the activity of the Reception
live to every one who wished to view it on H.E.N. channel 3. Keeping
with tradition, the Board of Trustees sponsored the Residents' Christmas
Party complete with a formal dinner and enteretainment which included
the appearance of Santa Claus, again happily portrayed by Worshipful
Ulysses G. Patropulos for the 16th year. Also the East Bay Past Matrons
Association reserved the third Saturday in August for their "Jam and Jelly
Day." For more than 70 years this part of our Masonic family has spent
the day with us, bringing many donated items, including a check in sufficient amount to purchase our year's supply of jams and jellies. Also, in
December they annually bring individualized Christmas gifts for the residents; as do many other Masonic affiliated groups. It is our pleasure to

of the 1983 Annual Communication. Prior to entering the Home many of
the men and women had no opportunity to attend the Annual Communication; while some of the Brethren appreciate the chance to continue
their years of attendance, being past officers of their Lodge and/or of
Grand Lodge.
Additional traditions at the Home include the celebration of Holidays
and certain "Theme" days. Among the more popular ones this year were
"Roaring 20's," "Hobo Day" and "Country Fair." Imaginations run wild
as costumes are created because prizes are awarded for the appropriate
(the Worst-Dressed Hobo was acknowledged). Entertainment, decorations, and food are all presented in keeping with the theme. Entertainment
at the Hobo Day was furnished by a small group of pseudo-professionals
consisting of several administrative staff and two residents. Through the
efforts of the Activities and Maintenance departments, the Home was
transformed into an old-time carnival setting on "Country Fair" day and
the activities offered were nostalgic for all. Included were the usual games
of chance or skill, a cotton candy machine, and a "dunk tank" manned
by certain members of administration who became targets for anyone who
could toss a ball more than three feet.

of belonging to a larger family. And I personally express my gratitude to
the Board of Trustees for their continued guidance and support, their
ability to implement change where needed, and their visionary plans as
they strive to provide the very best in care and services for our Family.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF THE ADMINISTRATOR
COVINA HOME
1983-1984
It is with continued pleasure that I submit this, my fourth, annual report
to the Grand Lodge. Each year brings more excitement as our Children's
Home continues to grow in both quality of service and population.
Significant changes have been implemented over these last several years.
This past year we have continued to concentrate on residential services
including health, hygiene, education, and various activities. As our population continues to grow, we must be ever attentive to our organization.
We must continue to provide a caring residential environment, but with
that internal organization required of any group endeavor.
Space and time ptevent me from listing the names of those many individuals who have been especially supportive of our Home. Nor those
Lodges and other Masonic Groups who never fail to remember the children. Each of you are fine examples of Masonic Charity. With your perpetual acts of love comes an equal measure of our gratitude.
So much gratitude is deserved by our dedicated Board of Trustees.
These brethren continue to provide the wisdom and leadership without
which our Homes could not survive. Through the wisdom of our Trustees,
and the strength of the Masonic Fraternity, we have served these following
children:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Our current population consists of 37 boys and 21 girls, for a total of
58. Our youngest child is three years of age and the oldest is eighteen.
We'll have 17 elementary school students, 20 junior high students, 21 high
school students. Our children attend the public schools in the Charter Oak
School District.
I encourage you to read the annual report of our Trustees which will
provide more detailed information about our operations in Covina.
In addition to reviewing the written reports, I encourage you, as do our
Trustees, to personally visit our Homes. The following groups within the
Masonic Family have visited the Children's Home during fiscal year 1983/4.

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

128

Respectfully submitted,
JoHN A. RosE, Administrator

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board is pleased to submit its 52nd
Annual Report covering the fiscal year ending June 30, 1984. Through
the enthusiasm and diligence of the Board Members and the commitment
of the Brethren to the residents of our two Homes, contributions to the
Endowment Fund have exceeded one and one half million dollars.

Income from the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund amounted to
$4,619,035.65 which amount was transferred to the operating account of
our two Homes. This income is an extremely and vitally important factor
in providing the Homes' Trustees with the funds necessary to maintain the
quality of care afforded to the residents of both of our Homes.

NOTE: We are pleased to report that 51.43% of our membership chose
to participate in this program. We are sure that this percentage of participation will continue to rise as the displayers which were sent to all Masonic Temples and Masters begin to be used. Among several innovations
this year, these displayers contain a short message pertinent to our two
Masonic Homes and many addressed, postage-paid envelopes. As these
contributions are received, the donor is sent a packet containing a similar
message, photographs of the Homes and grounds and additional contribution envelopes for use in making contributions throughout the year.
Other new ideas introduced in 1984 are memorial gifts credited to Lodges
for Honor Roll purposes and donation envelopes included as a center-fold
in the Freemason magazine. It is hoped that more and more Brethren and

HONOR ROLL TABS AND CERTIFICATES

more average per member, tabs will be presented to the Lodge following
the Annual Communication, by a member of the Endowment board. For
those Lodges which have attained Honor Roll status for the first time,
certificates and tabs will also be presented in like manner.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

CoNCLUSION

Our sincere and grateful thanks to Grand Master E. Arthur Haglund
and to the Grand Lodge officers and committeemen, all of whom have
been most supportive of the Endowment Program. We also wish to thank
the Masters, Wardens and Secretaries of the Lodges for their efforts in
furthering this worthy program.
We extend a special word of thanks to the 92,355 Brothers who, throug_h
their generosity, contributed $1,500,203.10 to the Endowment Fund this
past year.
We appreciate the splendid assistance we have received from the Gra~d
Secretary's office under the leadership of Grand Secretary Robert A. Khnger assisted by Assistant Grand Secretary Clare W. "Bud" Wilson, Jr. and
Brother Fran Lewis.
My personal thanks to the members of the Endowment Board for dedicated efforts which have again made this year an outstanding one.
Respectfully submitted,

Master, administer the quarterly editing and distribution of the California
Freemason, an official publication of the Grand Lodge.
In its 31st year of publication, nearly 19,000,000 copies have been distributed to the members of California Lodges, to the Grand Lodges of
other jurisdictions, and to paid subscribers. From time to time the magazine is quoted in publication of foreign Grand Lodges.
One of the important purposes of the California Freemason is to keep
the members of California Masonic Lodges fully informed of the events
of Grand Lodge, the activities of the Masonic Homes of California, U. S.
Constitution Observances, California Masonic Foundation, Public Schools
Week and events within Lodges: Hiram Awards, Widows Nights, Layman's Nights, and more. Its goal is to help maintain the high principles
and tenets of Freemasonry.
Since a two-year subscription fee of $2.00 will bring the magazine to
friends and families of California Masons, gift orders are encouraged as
a means of communicating the goals and purposes of our ancient and
honorable Fraternity to the general public.

REPORT OF SOJOURNERS COMMITTEE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

The Grand Lodge Committee on Sojourners is extending the hand of
fellowship, brotherly love and fraternal greetings to Sojourning Masons
residing in this Masonic Jurisdiction. Their endeavors in locating and getting acquainted with Sojourning Masons, inviting them to attend a local
California Lodge, inviting them to attend Sojourner Meetings, as well as
regular meetings, and finally affiliating with a local Masonic Lodge have
been successful and most encouraging.
The Committee members have been successful in many Lodges having
the Master appoint a Lodge Committee on Sojourners to work also with
the Grand Lodge Committee member. Many Sojourner Masons are
pleased and happy to be invited and asked to affiliate with a local Lodge
in the area in which they live.
The members of the Lodges are asked to register the names of Sojourners they know and to have them listed with the Lodge Sojourner Committee. The Committee is requested to make monthly reports at their
Lodge Stated meeting.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Sojourner Committee is composed of Past Masters and their efforts
and interest are most gratifying and the results being obtained are encouraging and well worthwhile.
Where possible, the Sojourner Committee is to work with the Masonic
Service Bureaus, and it is requested through this Annual Report that all
Masons that read this brief report will be concerned and interested and
endeavor to get acquainted with Sojourner Masons they meet in their
normal Masonic work as well as Masons they meet in the Scottish Rite,
York Rite, Shrine, High Twelve Clubs and any other Concordant Masonic
Body.
.
We do not have a Sojourner Committee member in every city in California or Hawaii so it is important that all Masonic Lodges appoint a
Lodge Committee to work on the Sojourner campaign, get acquainted
with Sojourner Masons, invite them to their respective Lodges and invite
them to affiliate with their particular Lodge. All Masons should know that
the California Grand Lodge permits Dual memberships, so it is not necessary for Sojourner Masons to drop out of their Mother Lodges in order
to affiliate with a California Masonic Lodge. Five State Grand Lodges do
not permit Dual Memberships; namely, Tennessee, Pennsylvania, West
Virginia, Missouri and Mississippi.
The Sojourner Committee has been active since 1981 and has brought
in at least 200 Sojourner Masons to California and Hawaii Lodges by
affiliation. Not only the Sojourner Committee can assist in bringing in
Sojourner Masons; every Mason can make a difference-You!

REPORT OF TRUSTEES
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
hereby submits its 29th Annual Report.
At the close of the 1983 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, the
Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple held its
organization meeting as required by the California Masonic Code, nominating and electing the following officers for the ensuing year:
Stanley M. Cazneaux President
Robert 0. West, P.G.M. Vice-President

John A. Sickenberger Treasurer
Robert A. Klinger Secretary

The California Masonic Memorial Temple serves as a patriotic monument and memorial, open to the public, commemorating the members of
the armed services of the United States and of the Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California, who gave
their lives in battle during World War II.
With this definition in mind, it is incumbent upon the Trustees to maintain the facility and to permit it to function within the spirit associated
with a historic monument of great Masonic significance. The Trustees can
report with confidence that all the persons associated with the operation
and maintenance of the California Masonic Memorial Temple have faithfully discharged their duties.
At the 1969 Annual Communication, a Resolution was adopted requesting the Temple Board of Trustees to acquire the two properties on
Pine Street directly behind our beautiful stained glass lobby window and
prepare plans for the development of the property. The Board was also
required to present any proposed plans to Grand Lodge for approval prior
to any construction. Over the next several years, plans were developed
for an addition to our Temple which would house a Library and Museum,
later to be known as the Learning Center.
In 1972, the Temple Board reported to Grand Lodge that the feasibility
report, as well as the schematic drawings for the expansion of the Temple
had been carefully studied and reviewed. The Committee on Finance and
the Committee on Policy and General Purposes also reviewed the report,
and it was their unanimous opinion not to proceed with the plan at that

157

1. Refurbishing of apartments as they become vacant, including remodeling of kitchens and bathrooms and upgrading of electrical and
plumbing systems.
2. Re-roofing of the four apartment houses including removal of old
roofs.
3. Installation of an access control system to the front doors for the
security of our tenants.
4. Hired Ross Architectural Group for suggested color schemes which
would be most suitable to the Victorian style of the buildings. We
have currently let bids for the painting contract.
It continues to be the policy of the Trustees and of all the employees
of the Temple to maintain this building which attracts the public. Because
of our exceptional location and the superb acoustical quality of our Auditorium, we continue to attract concerts, lectures and musical plays. Business organizations, governmental agencies and professional associations
find our Temple to be an excellent choice and return year after year.
During 1983, we negotiated a new lease with Metropolitan Parking Systems for the operation of our Garage. We had high expectations that the
new arrangements would be satisfactory not only for the Temple, but also
for the Lessee. Those expectations have been realized with a 30% increase
in revenue for the Temple. The painting of the entire Garage area was
completed early this year. Re-striping of the Garage stalls resulted in an
increase of 35 additional parking spaces.
The Trustees are pleased to announce the continuation of our policy of
providing free parking to our delegates during the official transactions of
Grand Lodge at the Annual Communications. In addition, we have provided decorative plants and additional seating in our Temple Lobby during
Grand Lodge Week.
Although the maintenance of our Temple requires a continued expenditure of monies, your Trustees are pleased to report that we are still able
this year to donate $40,000.00 to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund
. accordance with our By-Laws.

During the period July 1, 1983-June 30, 1984, we received 2,355 requests for scholarship awards. The necessary application forms and letters
of instruction were sent in response to each of those requests. Each application was processed, reviewed, and a determination made of the need
and worthiness of the applicant.
We awarded 123 scholarships in the total sum of $60,000.00 from the
General Fund and 45 scholarships in the sum of $22,500.00 from the
Amaranth Fund. Awards were also made from the Mendenhall, Robinson
and LaSuer funds consistent with the provisions of those funds stipulated
by the donors thereof.
As of June 30, 1984, the Foundation has awarded from the General
Fund 841 scholarships to needy and worthy students in a total sum of
$473,850.00; without having expended any Capital Funds.
Due to the great need for scholarships and the resulting demand on
available funds, we have not been in a position to make grants for charitable, scientific or other worthwhile and deserving causes. We believe
these are well within the scope of the Foundation and should be included
in our activities to achieve the full purpose of our existence. It is the hope
and expectancy of your Board of Trustees that in the near future our
financial position will permit the resumption of these activities.
The Most Worshipful Grand Master having delegated to your Foundation, as the appropriate agency of Grand Lodge, the conduct of the campaign for contribution of California and Hawaiian Masons to the Statue
of Liberty Restoration Project, we are pleased to report that as.of October
5, 1984 we have received 16,960 contributions, totaling $385,002.81, for
that Project. A substantial part of that number were from Concordant
Bodies and their members. Therefore, our participation is well below ten
percent. If we stated that such participation is disappointing, it would be
a gross understatement. The task of recording, accounting and acknowledging those contributions has been and is monumental. Untold man hours
have been devoted to that task by members of your Board of Trustees and
others. The task is not finished, and all members of Grand Lodge should
volunteer their efforts to bring this most worthwhile project to a complete
and successful conclusion.

REPORT OF CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Trustees of the California Masonic Foundation report as follows:
The work of your Board is current and has been promptly and efficiently
dispatched. Your Trustees have worked diligently and effectively to
achieve the purposes of the Foundation, and to make them known_ to ~he
Brethren of this Jurisdiction and to encourage its support by contnbution
and donation.
It can no longer be said that the California Masonic Foundation is the
best kept secret in Freemasonry. Your Trustees and their representatives
have made over 800 appearances on behalf of the Foundation, before
Constituent Lodges, Officers Associations, Masonic information meetings, Concordant and affiliated bodies and organizations. Information and
activities have been disseminated to the Lodges, and the "Freemason" has
published articles and news items. If any member of a Lodge of thi~ Jurisdiction is still unaware of the Foundation, its purposes and achievements, he must be both deaf and blind.
During this reporting period we have received donations and contributions totaling $30,646.00. Appropriate acknowledgment thereof was
made to the donors, and to the families of those persons in whose memory
many of these contributions were made. Since 1974 our capital funding
has been increased by $188,000.00 from these contributions and donations.
The investments, income and expense of the Foundation are set forth
in the Report of the Grand Treasurer and are not, therefore, repeated
here. Direct Trustee expense was approximately 8.2% of total income for
the reporting period. Total administration expense, including United
States income tax, was 13.1 % of total income.
The members of Grand Lodge should be minded that the Foundation
has not received any funds from Grand Lodge by way of per capita tax or
assessment and that in fact no funds, including the original capitalization
of the Foundation, came from any per capita tax, assessment or out of
direct Grand Lodge funds. They should also be minded that the Trustees
of the Foundation have not expended any capital funds. All awards, grants
and administrative expense have been paid from income or from contri-

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Distinguished Guests and Brethren.
The Charters Committee for the 1984 Masonic Year has attempted a new
approach to our declining trend in membership by endeavoring to assist
in correction of situations which have influenced Lodges to contemplate
consolidation. The predominant cause for Lodge discouragement appears
to be in finding dedicated Masons to progress through the line of offices.
We feel that the Leadership Workshops offered throughout the Jurisdiction can help change this picture, and we urge the Executive Board to
continue this program. Our efforts are not yet conclusive, because we
must maintain a wait and see period to determine if the dilemmas have
been resolved to where the respective Lodges remain in the mainstream
of Masonry.
No Lodges were held over under Dispensation from the 1983 Communication, and no new Lodges have been Instituted during the current
year. I am pleased to inform you that a Dispensation has been granted to
Orange County Research Lodge now meeting at La Habra Masonic Temple, and it will be Instituted in the near future.
The King Kalakaua Masonic Club in Honolulu, formed in June of 1983,
has progressed to forty (40) members, and has distributed the required 45
day notice of intention to form a Daylight Lodge. A petition for Dispensation is expected by the latter part of October.
We have made a concerted effort to contact concordant bodies throughout the Jurisdiction to locate Sojourning and inactive Masons to encourage

The Committee on Travel Allowances submits the following report covering the 135th Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
Those entitled to travel allowances are the Master, or in his absence,
the ranking Warden, or in the absence of the Master and Wardens, the
duly Elected Representative in accordance with Section 1148, California
Masonic Code. Past Grand Masters, not on Committees, will be reimbursed as provided in Section 1150, California Masonic Code. In accordance with Section 1148a, California Masonic Code, when a Master and
Warden from the same Lodge are present at an Annual Communication,
and one of said officers serves on a Grand Lodge Committee entitled to
travel and expense reimbursement, he shall be reimbursed under Section
1150, California Masonic Code. The other officer shall receive reimbursement under Section 1148, California Masonic Code, as the officer representing his Lodge on the floor of Grand Lodge.
Mileage from the various points within the State of California to San
Francisco has been taken from the published records of the California
State Automobile Association. Mileage from points in the State of Hawaii
to San Francisco has been taken from the published reports of Air Lines
in accordance with Section 1148, California Masonic Code. No compensation is allowed to members from San Francisco or the immediate vicinity.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
GABON

The Grande Loge Du Gabon, heretofore operating as a District Grand
Lodge under the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise, was by Most Wor-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

shipful Jean Mons, Grand Master, consecrated and constituted into a Regular Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of Gabon on November
12th, 1983 in Libreville, Gabon.
The six (6) Lodges composing the Grand Lodge were all Chartered and
Constituted by the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise (French National
Grand Lodge) and were constituted into a District Grand Lodge in 1980
with the President of Gabon, Most Worshipful Omar Bongo as District
Grand Master, who now has been installed as Grand Master of the Independent Grand Lodge.
Gabon, the Gabonese Republic, is located on the Atlantic Coast of
central Africa, bordered by Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon, and the
Congo. The Country is made up of nine Provinces with its Capital at
Libreville which has a population of 250,000. The whole Country covers
an area of 103,347 square miles (about the size of Colorado) and has a
total population of 750,000. The school system has twenty-six teachers per
1,000 students, and more than 75% of ages 5 to 19 are in school. The
official language is French. France established control over the region in
the second half of the 19th century, and Gabon became independent in
1960. It is one of the most prosperous countries in Africa due to its rich
and abundant natural resources, all watered by the Ogouue River system,
private foreign investment and government sponsored development programs.
Right Worshipful Robert L. Dillard, Jr., Past Grand Master of Texas
and Secretary-Treasurer of the Commission for Recognition of the Grand
Masters Conference of North America, at the invitation of Grand Master
Mons attended the ceremonies as an observer. Brother Dillard reported
a very cordial reception, with impressive ceremonies of consecration and
installation attended by about 300 Masons including representatives of

IRAN

When organized Freemasonry in Iran was destroyed by the revolution
of 1979, most o~ the individual Masons (1,035 members of 43 Lodges) fled
to ~ther _countnes, many of them to the United States and particularly to
Cahforma where they found the hand of Brotherly love extended in friendship'. relief and truth, ~i~h a sincere desire to assist them in any way
pos.sible. Some of them v!sited our Lodges and applied for affiliation while
their documents were still current and valid. Many arrived without any
documents, so the Grand Lodge of California established an arrangement
through the Commission for Recognition of the Conference of Grand
Masters of North America to verify their membership under the Grand
Lodg~ -~f Iran "Upon Hono_ur Alone" for the purpose of affiliation (not
for visiting as our law provides that any person entering a Lodge must
possess a currently dated certificate of good standing in a regular Lodge).
Many ha_ve taken advantage of this opportunity; others have applied for
.
and received the degrees in our Lodges.
In our effort to further our cooperation with these Brethren, Brother
Mohammad T. Fekri, an affiliated member of our Santa Monica Lodge
No. 307, was requested to arrange a meeting with Hossein Daftarian, the
~ast Grand Secretary o_f the Grand Lodge of Iran. This meeting was held
m Long Beach on Apnl 16, 1982, and, at the invitation of your Chairman,
was attended by Kenneth P. Elliott of the Committee, Brother Fekri, and
Brother ~a~tarian who bro~ght with him Amir Mansour Shahparaki who
was not _mvited: Shahparak1 attempted to dominate the meeting and (no
doubt did dommate Daftarian) made it quite evident that they did not
want the cooperation we were rendering, but the full right of visitation
and the establishment of their own Lodges under their jurisdiction. The
Doctrine of Exclusive Jurisdiction was explained to them as well as our
laws concerning the creation of new Lodges, and even though they seemed
disappointed, they agreed to cooperate.
We assured Brother Daftarian that, with the assistance of Brother Fekri
we .~ou~d continue our efforts to assist all former members in Iran
venflcatl?n through ou~ Grand Secretary as in the past, and the meeting
closed with agreement m apparent peace and harmony, since which time
not "word one" has ever been heard directly from Brother Daftarian or
Shahparaki.
Brother Daftarian was referred to Right Worshipful Robert L. Dillard,
Jr., Secretary of the Commission for Recognition of the Grand Masters
Conference of North America, and after some time did contact Brother
Dillard who confirmed the Doctrine of Exclusive Jurisdiction. Brother

b;

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Daftarian offered to verify membership and cooperate with Brother Dillard, but nothing significant took place until late in 1983.
Subsequent to the meeting of April 16, 1982, it was reported to the
undersigned that meetings of Iranian Masons were being held in Beverly
Hills where large amounts of money were being collected (like $12 to
$1500 per person) to further their organization and for charitable work.
Then, in October 1983, it was reported that a new Grand Lodge of Iran
would be organized in New York in November or December. Shortly
thereafter a call was received from an Iranian Mason (not a member in
California) residing in Beverly Hills, who advised that the new Grand
Lodge of Iran would be constituted in New York on December 10, 1983,
having received permission from the "High Council" of the conference of
Scottish Rite of the World at a recent meeting in Istanbul, Turkey, and he
had been directed by Hossein Dafterian, who would be Grand Master, to
obtain from me, "the Scottish Rite Ritual" for opening and Constitution.
I advised the caller, Moyed Gharemani, that I could have nothing to do
with such an activity and that he or anyone else who did would automatically sever their relationship with "Regular Freemasonry." The proposed
organization was executed in the Masonic Hall of the Grand Lodge of
New York on December 10, 1983 with approximately 60 persons present,
including Iranian Masons from the United States and other countries, and
a representative of the Grand Lodge of New York and other guests. This
would appear to be a usurping of power by a small minority of the estimated 500 Iranian Masons in the United States, approximately 300 of
whom are estimated to be in California, and immediate criticism has been
expressed by former officers of the Grand Lodge of Iran.
On or about June 6, 1984 our Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful Robert
A. Klinger, received a letter of invitation from the "Grand Lodge of Iran
(in exile)" to attend their semi-annual meeting to be held on June 16,
1984 in the Masonic Hall of the Grand Lodge of New York, as did other
Masonic leaders, but none are known to have responded except the Grand
Lodge of New York. According to reports, approximately 60 people attended the meeting in New York, quite a number of whom were from
California, some of whom are Grand Officers of the Grand Lodge of Iran,
(new) and members of California Lodges, some of whom were Iranian
Masons from other countries, and others who were not before Masons.
At least one who was not before a Mason was, for a generous donation,
presented a Certificate indicating that he is a Master Mason in good
standing and could use the certificate to visit or affiliate with Lodges in
America.
Your Chairman is in possession of a letter dated July 26, 1984 signed
by Nematollah Raeen as Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Iran,
from which I quote the 4th paragraph:
"48 Iranian Masons whose names are reflected in the Grand Lodge
register, participated in the semi-annual Communication. These comprise
22 Iranian Past Masters, including the Grand Officers of the Grand Lodge
of Iran; 24 Masters (representing their respective Lodges) who had all
been raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason in Iran and 2 other

Iranian Masters who had attained to this privilege in the United States of
America; namely Brother Alireza Tabatabai from Santa Monica Lodge
and Brother Bahram Raeen, a second degree Mason of Lodge Hateff No.
33, from Van Nuys Lodge No. 450 of California. On that day a number
of the Brethren who had not paid their dues, each paid U. S. $50.00 to
the Grand Treasurer covering the membership dues for 1984 and 1985. A
few Brethren expressed interest in becoming life members. U. S. $199.00
was collected for alms. No other payments were made as far as the Grand
Lodge of Iran is concerned."
There are a lot of good Masons in California of Iranian descent, and
many of them have not yet affiliated with a Lodge in California. So as the
majority should not be caused to suffer because of the acts of the minority,
it is recommended that the present policy of clearing Applications for
Affiliation through the Grand Secretary before reception be continued,
and that no recognition whatsoever be extended to the new Grand Lodge
of Iran (in exile) constituted in New York on December 10, 1983, or to
any document issued by it.
I move the approval and adoption of this portion of the report together
with the above recommendation.

duly seconded and upon a vote taken, was Adopted.
NEW JERSEY

On February 7th, 1984 Gothic Lodge No. 270, Hamilton Square, New
Jersey, received a Petition for Degrees and Membership from Mr. Danny
Thomas (also known as Amos Jacobs) with full knowledge that Mr.
Thomas was and is a legal resident of the State of California. Notwithstanding this fact, and without any waiver from a Lodge in California, and
over the objection of our Grand Master and Grand Secretary, the then
Grand Master of New Jersey issued a Dispensation authorizing Gothic
Lodge to receive and act upon the petition. Thus the petition under date
of February 7, 1984 was acted upon February 20, 1984 with a favorable
ballot, and the three degrees of Freemasonry were conferred upon Mr.
Thomas in the Scottish Rite Cathedral in Trenton, New Jersey on March
15, 1984.
Now, our Grand Master has for several months pursued a prudent,
charitable, fraternal course of endeavor with the leaders of the Grand
Lodge of New Jeresey to correct their errors in the best interest of Universal Freemasonry in general and New Jersey and California in particular,
without effect, and finally with discreet courage executed the only option
open to him.
In view of above, it is the opinion of your Committee on Recognition
of Foreign Grand Lodges that the Decision of the Grand Master in withdrawing recognition of the Grand Lodge Free and Accepted Masons of
New Jersey is proper and should be approved by this Grand Lodge.

ITALY
Notwithstanding the problems confronting Regular Freemasonry in Italy, the Grand Orient continues to progress, increase the membership and
establish new Lodges. During the past six years 73 new Lodges have been
constituted.
SPAIN
In May this year it was learned that Worshipful Victor Carbone was
conducting a tour of California Masons and their ladies through Spain, so
a banquet was arranged in Barcelona to which the Grand Master of Spain,
Most Worshipful Luis Salat Gusils and his lady, and Worshipful Count
Talarwitz Podolsky and his lady were invited as guests. Brother Carbone
reports a very pleasant and productive fraternal evening. So well were the
impressions made that on the Tour's arrival in Madrid a few days later
Count Podolsky was there to reciprocate. The Universality of Regular
Freemasonry is being maintained in Spain.
AUSTRIA
The Grand Lodge of Austria executed an elaborate and impressive ceremony from April 26th to 29th, 1984 celebrating the Bicentenary of the
founding of the Grand Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of
Austria in 1784, and to mark the 250th anniversary of the introduction of
Freemasonry into the area. The ceremonies were graced with many outstanding events and closed with a special performance at Vienna State
Opera of "The Magic Flute."
THE UNIVERSALITY OF FREEMASONRY
Our Grand Master and Grand Secretary are to be commended, and we
appreciate their interest in maintaining the Universality of Regular Freemasonry. We appreciate also the counsel and assistance of Right Worshipful Robert L. Dillard, Jr., Secretary-Treasurer of the Commission on Information for Recognition of the Grand Masters Conference of North
America, "always available when requested." We are appreciative and
grateful; the benefit is to Freemasonry.

REPORT OF
WELCOME AND INFORMATION COMMITTEE
FOR 1984 OLYMPIC GAMES
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
This Committee, created by the Grand Master for the purpose of welcome information and service to Masons and their families from around
the w'orld while visiting the XXIII Olympiad, commenced its work early
in the Masonic year. It reserved the telephone number, "MAS 0 N 84",
and working with the Grand Master, Grand Secretary, Public Relations
Committee, and the Los Angeles Masonic Press Club, distributed the
Grand Master's Proclamation along with news releases to our own Lodges,
to all Regular Grand Lodges of the World, to all Masonic Publications of
the world, and to selected News Media. A Grand Master's News Conference was held at the Greater Los Angeles Press Club. All of this proved
to be very effective as we received confirmation from many foreign countries as well as th~ United States of our project's publicity not only in the
Masonic Press, but also the international news media. A telephone call
was received from the Grand Lodge of Peru in Lima with the message
that they did not expect to have anyone attending in person but wished
us well in our undertaking.
The forefront of our project was the "Host and Information Center"
headquartered in the beautiful Scottish Rite Masonic Temple in Los Angeles where we received many visitors, both Masons and non-Masons,
from such places as Africa, India, China, Japan, The Philippines, Canada,
England, Scotland, Ireland, Italy, Chile, Peru, et. al. as well as ot?er
jurisdictions of the United States. Our California Brethren were also impressed and brought their non-Mason friends to view the displays, tour
the Lodge rooms, obtain information and receive literature on Freemasonry.
. .
.
Our Grand Master is to be commended for the leadership given to this
important project, especially the enhancement of the Public and Universal
Fraternal Relations of Freemasonry in general, and of California Masonry
in particular. A Brother writing in the Guest Book said it well, "Th~
Olympics display is fantastic and the person or persons who thought of it
has contributed greatly to the public relations of Masonry."

REPORT OF THE COMMITTE E ON
MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus is pleased to submit its
Annual Report on the operations and condition of the eighteen Masonic
Service Bureaus for the year ending June 30, 1984. The Committee is in
its 57th year.
The Right Worshipful Roy J. Henville, Deputy Grand Master, was appointed liaison officer. We have appreciated his support and assistance
during the year and his meeting with us .during our budget session.
The Committee is well aware of its responsibility in directing the operation of the Bureaus in a uniform manner. The Service Bureaus assist
the Sojourners, their widows and orphans, operate blood banks, arrange
and conduct funerals for deceased Masons, make investigations, assist in
the applications for the Masonic Hornes, visit sick and promote fraternal
relations with Sojourners.
NEW COMMITTEE MEMBERS
We welcomed to our Committee two new members, Ray H. Rookard,
a Past Master of Acalanes-Fellowship Lodge No. 480 and a former Inspector of the 158th Masonic District, and Henry M. Kirkland, a Past
Master and member of Blackmer Lodge No. 442. Both are honour men
in the concordant bodies.
Delmer W. May was appointed Chairman of the Committee by the Most
Worshipful Grand Master, E. Arthur Haglund.

MASONIC RELIEF ASSOCIATION OF THE U.S. AND CANADA
MEETINGS

The Committee held four meetings during the year. One was held during Grand Lodge Week which permitted members of the Bureaus and
Lodge officers to contact the Committee and receive help with their many
problems.
A regional meeting was held in Oakland on February 18, 1984. Thirty
members and guests of the Bureaus from Northern California attended.
Former Chairman of the Committee, Arthur R. Kirk, was the speaker.
A regional meeting was held in Los Angeles on March 24, 1984. Twentyeight officers and members of the Bureaus attended. Most Worshipful
Burton Meyers, Jr. was the guest speaker and spoke on the Bush Masonic
Memorial Fund.
On June 12, 1984, a meeting of the Committee was held in Pasadena at
the Scottish Rite Temple. The Deputy Grand Master, Right Worshipful
Roy J. Henville, attended this meeting and his advice and assistance were
appreciated. The Committee reviewed the annual Masonic Service Bureaus' Budgets for 1984-85 as well as other Committee business.
TAXES

All Bureaus have filed the required information return to the Internal
Revenue Service on Form 990 and the State Franchise Board on either
Form 199 or 199B. The Los Angeles Bureau prepares forms other than
the 990 and the 199. All Bureaus requiring tax returns have filed them on
schedule .
BUDGETS

Each Bureau presents a Budget for the approval of the Committee on
or before May 1 each year. The Budget covers the operating expenses and
income for the period starting July 1 and ending June 30. The Budget
recommends a per capita assessment to be collected from their member
Lodges.
The approved Budget covering the operation of the Bureaus increased
over the past year to a total estimated expense of $149,548.
BUSH MASONIC RELIEF

The Worshipful Ralph H. Head, President of the Bush Masonic Relief
Fund, and the Trustees provided the operating funds for the Bureaus
located in the greater Los Angeles Area. The contributions amounted to
64 per cent of the total Budget for the Eighteen Bureaus. The Masters,

Our Grand Lodge now holds membership in the Masonic Relief Association of the United States and Canada. The Association has many
functions including the correlation of the various forms of Masonic relief
throughout the United States and Canada. Our California Bureaus will
benefit from this membership.
We are pleased to report that the Executive Secretary of the Los Angeles Bureau, Lloyd V. Smith, is a Director of the Association.
ANNUAL REPORTS

All Bureaus have supplied the annual reports to the Committee. These
included the Election Report, Budget, Statistical and Financial Report,
Operating Expenses and Fixed Assets, as well as the Blood Bank reports.
The Bureaus conducted 152 Masonic Funeral Services for deceased Sojourners, made 314 visits to sick Sojourners, and conducted 131 investigations. The Executive Secretaries of the Bureaus assisted in preparing ~1
applications to Masonic Homes, some in this Jurisdiction and some m
other jurisdictions. Many requests for financial relief were received and
many were taken care of.

.

BLOOD BANKS

Several of our Bureaus operate blood banks for the benefit of the members' Lodges and Sojourners. During the year, 1,468 units of ?lood w~re
donated and over 1,832 units of blood were released to provide the important life support to our members, their families and ~ojou~ners. We
compliment the Bureaus and our members for supportmg this worthy
activity.
UNIFORM COMPACTS

A Uniform Compact is due from Tri Lodge No. 595, as this Lodge is a
consolidation of John Marshall Lodge No. 636 and Alexander Graham
Bell-Benjamin Franklin Lodge No. 595, one a member of the Los Angeles
Bureau and the other, the Santa Monica Bureau.
Also, a Compact is due from Palm-Adams Lodge No. 512. This Lodge
was the result of the merger of Palms Lodge No. 512 and West Adams
Lodge No. 565. Again, one Lodge belonged to the Los Angeles Bureau
and the other to the Santa Monica Bureau.

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Investment Committee reports on the condition of the various funds
of Grand Lodge and its entities. During the year the Committee meets
quarterly with its investment counselors. At each meeting an independent
investment organization reviews the performance of the funds on a comparative basis with funds of a similar nature throughout the United States.
Of primary importance to the Committee is the preservation of fund
principal and the highest rate of total return commensurate with safety.
There are three funds: Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, Masonic

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Homes General Fund and the Hugo M. Lorber Union City Home Fund,
which constitute 97% of the total investments.
Supervised by the Committee are other Grand Lodge funds: Grand
Lodge General Fund, California Masonic Memorial Temple, California
Masonic Foundation and Amaranth Fund, Pooled Income Fund and eighteen restricted-use funds of the Masonic Homes.
The market value of the total portfolio was $114,540,165 compared with
$112,283,000 a year earlier. The 1983-84 annual yield from the total funds
invested was 10.1 % .
Fixed income securities including government and corporate bonds composed 73% of the total portfolio. The remainder consisted of common
stocks and convertible bonds.
The Pooled Income Fund is important to the Masonic Homes. On June
30, 1984, the Fund had a market value of $1,588,932. The annual yield
based on the original investment was 10.5%. The Pooled Income Fund
provides an opportunity for the Masons in California and Hawaii and
others to establish a lifetime income for themselves and one-time designated beneficiaries. Certain tax advantages accrue to the contributor.
The concern and generosity of the Masons of California and Hawaii
and their friends have been responsible for the accumulation of the assets
of the several Grand Lodge funds. The income from these funds help to
finance the operations of the Masonic Homes at Union City and Covina
and furnish support for the many charitable activities and educational
grants of Grand Lodge.
During the past year the Investment Committee has exercised the utmost prudence and care in the management of the funds. The investments
rank among the highest in quality and a conservative investment policy
has resulted in a satisfactory total return.

One special meeting was held to plan a display of artifacts at Grand
Lodge in October.
Seventeen Lodges held degrees in the Temple this year, one group of
Eastern Star Grand Officers and other small groups were welcomed. With
the Fallon House Theatre re-opened, we expect more next year. Both the
Temple and theatre are air conditioned.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON COMMERCIALISM
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
As our country's economy has improved, the number of requests for
fund raising assistance has decreased. There is one form of fund raising
that Masonic Lodges and concordant bodies are doing, that is the sale of
commemorative coins.
To observe a Lodge's or concordant organization's special event such as
a seventy-fifth or hundredth anniversary, a commemorative coin is struck
and offered for sale to the Brethren. The · offer to sell is done through
Masonic publications and by word of mouth.
In order for these sales to be valid for California and Hawaiian Masonic
bodies, the Grand Master must approve the sale. The announcement of
the sale of these coins must be made only in Masonic publications. The
public must not be solicited to purchase these coins. The proceeds from
the sale may be used for Lodge purposes.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE
ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your hard working Grand Lodge Public Schools Committee of thirty
(30) members continued many of the programs of the past and implemented changes where necessary. It attempted to be of the utmost assistance to the Lodges in this Jurisdiction to keep the Craft involved in the
support of public schools.
We had the support and encouragement of our Grand Master, Most
Worshipful E. Arthur Haglund, and his corps of Officers. To them and
the Grand Secretary and particularly Marian Thomas, we express our
thanks for the cooperation with and understanding of our Committee.
Our thanks to Right Worshipful John W. Driskell for his continuous
support and encouragement. The continued cooperation of the District
Inspectors is greatly appreciated by the entire Committee.
We continue our concept of having a division coordinator in each of our
seven divisions with several committeemen working under each coordinator. With this concept we are able to assure personal contact with each
Lodge in California and Hawaii.
The Grand Master proclaimed Public Schools Week during April and
encouraged all Lodges to contact their local public schools to designate a
period during April as Public Schools Week in their locality based on the
excellent theme, "Quality and Excellence in Public Education-The Key
to America's Future." The cooperation of school boards, administrators,
and public officials resulted in numerous pronouncements and proclamations of Public Schools Week reaching far and wide to the general public.
The Grand Master's promotion of the Masonic Leadership Workshops
and the Masonic Festivals gave this Committee many additional opportunities to promote public schools' support and understanding among the
Craft.
Two full Committee meetings were held during this past year, one in
November at the Airport Hyatt Hotel in Los Angeles and the second
meeting on Tuesday during Grand Lodge Week in San Francisco.
The spirit and cooperation of the Committee continues to be excellent
for sharing ideas and becoming knowledgeable of each other's talents. The

185

GENERAL PROMOTION AND PuBLICITY

Our Committee printed posters, pamphlets, and appreciation certificates. We provided almost 60,000 six-inch rulers printed with centimetqs
and inches and the 1984 theme for the Lodges to purchase and distribute
to the elementary schools in their areas.
Samples of the 1984 materials were distributed to the Senior Wardens
at the Public Schools Booth on "G" floor during Grand Lodge Week along
with order forms and return envelopes. Order forms and return envelopes
also went to the Masters and Lodge Secretaries in January. The response
from the Lodges ordering materials was gratifying as the supply was depleted. No charge was made for the pamphlets. Many School Districts
gave a pamphlet to every student to take home.
In December 1984, your Committee mailed four 200 word articles about
our public schools to the incoming Masters with the suggestion that the
articles be included in the Lodges' January, February, March and April
Lodge bulletins. In April we mailed another article for the May bulletin.
These articles were well received and used by many Lodges in their bulletins or paraphrased by the Masters in their Master's Message for those
particular months.
Public Schools Observance copy for broadcasting was delivered to radio
stations and cable companies in California by mail, and committeemen
along with a letter from the Grand Master urging use of the copy during
April as spot an9ouncements. Also, slides depicting our 1984 theme and
copy were delivered to the television stations in our Jurisdiction for airing
and viewing during April. In general the cooperation of the stations was
gratifying in the rural areas, but still left much to be desired in the larger
areas.
Many local essay contests, poster contests, spelling bees, science fairs,
etc. were held throughout our Jurisdiction on a Lodge, District and area
basis with excellent participation and enthusiasm. It is hoped that someday
statewide contests can be conducted. Your Committee has found that
where the children are deeply involved in any school/Lodge observance,
the enthusiasm and attendance of the public and also our Brethren and
their families is excellent.
We mailed to the newspapers in California a picture of our Grand Master and Bill Honig, State Superintendent of Public Instruction, receiving
the California Legislative Resolution designating Public Schools Week
during April by Brothers Senator Ralph Dills, Senator Walter Stiern, Senator Nicholas Petris, and Senator Ray Johnson. Along with the picture,
we sent a mat of our poster, a copy of the Resolution, a copy of our Grand
Master's Proclamation, a biography of the men in the picture and a news
release about Public Schools Week and our Masonic involvement in our
Public Schools.

Questionnaires were sent to all Masters in May seeking their opinions
and information on their Lodges' participation in Public Schools Weekobservances. Many constructive thoughts were expressed by over 60 percent of the Lodges reporting. Many local newspaper and radio features
were employed by the Lodges and Districts. Outstanding types of observances were held locally, but are too numerous to list individually in the
report. Brief descriptions of some of the Lodges' most successful events
will be given to the Senior Wardens during Grand Lodge Week. Almost
all types of observances are noted in the Public Schools Guidelines (green)
in the Lodge Manual. It is urged that all Masters, Wardens and Lodge
Public School Committeemen read these guidelines.
In February, our Grand Master wrote to the leadership of all concordant
and affiliated Masonic organizations in California and Hawaii soliciting
their support for the April Public Schools Observances. The Grand Master's letter, containing his Proclamation and the California Legislative Resolution, was sent to each High Twelve Club, Sciots, Pyramid, Eastern Star
Chapter, Scottish Rite and Shrine Temple in our Jurisdiction. The PTA
and United Americans for Public Schools both published the Grand Master's Proclamation and reproduced the 1984 Public Schools poster in their
April publications. The California Teachers Association, the California
School Board Association and the California School Administrators Asso~iation supported Public Schools Week in their March and April Magazmes. Our materials were sent to some of these organizations' Conventions for display. Consideration will be given in the future to actually
having a manned booth at these Conventions.

Our Grand Master and his cabinet has continued to look for new ways

with the California School Board Association, we will co-sponsor a "Hall

The members of the Public Schools Committee have been receiving a
Legislative Report weekly from the California School Board Association
News to help keep us abreast of the Legislature's position and bills affecting public education.

MEETING WITH ST ATE OFFICIALS

Your Grand Master and Public Schools Committee Chairman met with
Mr. Bill Honig, State of California Superintendent of Public Instruction,
in his office in Sacramento. The meeting was most productive and in the
true spirit of cooperation. Mr. Honig was particularly appreciative and
cognizant of the fact that the Masons support the concept of Public Education. Your Grand Master and Public Schools Committee Chairman concur with the principles expressed by Mr. Honig in his education reform
bill SB 813. Mr. Honig expressed his thanks to our Grand Master and the
Lodges of California for their support of SB 813.
Mr. Honig issued a letter in January 1984 to all District and County
Superintendents advising them that the local Masonic Lodges would be
contacting them regarding mutual participation in the Public Schools Week
functions in April. Your Committee made copies of Mr. Honig's letter and
mailed it to all Masters. Mr. Honig issued a news release to all forms of
the media on April 1, 1984 encouraging Public Schools Week Observances
and sent a copy to all District and County Superintendents. The annual
meeting with the Superintendent of Public Instruction should be continued.
In Hawaii, the local Public Schools Committee has expressed a deep
concern about April not being an acceptable time for their Public Schools

CONCLUSION

The Committee on Public Education has functioned in 1984 under a
new Chairman who wishes to express his many thanks to Robert
McDonald who chaired the Committee for several years in outstanding
style. His cooperation was invaluable.
We continue to develop new approaches for supporting our Public
Schools and need to encourage all Lodges, big or small, to do their part.
We are pleased to assist all Lodges when called upon. We strive for successes and share them with other Lodges.

Blue Shield of California presently underwrites the health insurance
program provided for the employees of the Grand Lodge of California,
Masonic Homes of California, and the California Memorial Temple Association. The estimated annual premium is projected to be $162,000.
Claims paid ending December 31, 1983 totalled $159,400. Claims paid
January 1, 1984 through June 30, 1984 totalled $51,899. The most recent
loss runs are encouraging, and with continued signs of improvement it is
felt that there should not be an increase in the health premium currently
being charged.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
LODGE RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A. M . of California:
This year has been an extremely busy one for your Lodge Resources
Development Committee. The development of the Grand Master's
Achievement Award started the year out with a bang. This award was
developed around a program used by the Grand Lodge of Wisconsin and
was modified to meet our Jurisdiction 's requirements. The program consists of four basic areas: Lodge Officer Development, Programs, Masonic
Responsibility, and Social Responsibility. Compliance with the award's
requirements indicates that a Lodge is healthy and has a well rounded
program for its members. To date we have 79 Lodges that have responded
with applications for this award and 61 Lodges have qualified. The award,
a plaque that can be hung in the Lodge, will be presented for the first
time to the eligible Lodges by the Grand Master at the 1984 Annual
Communication.
The award itself is not the important part of the program. What is
important is that the Lodge begins to establish c. strong, well rounded
program for its members; one that involves the individual mem bers of the
Lodge in their Lodge activities. This, of course , can be accomplished by
working to achieve the requirements of the Grand Master's Achievement
Award. For Lodges that are having problems, the Brethren will find that
if they sincerely try to accomplish the tasks outlined in the application ,
the Lodge will begin to turn around, attendance will improve and Officers
and new members will be easier to find. Attempting to comply with t he
requirements of the Grand Master's Achievement Award will automatically begin to involve the membership of the Lodge and start the Lodge
on the way to recovery. Remember, a strong Lodge is an active Lodge ,
one that involves its members in its activities. If your Lodge didn't earn ,
or apply for, the award this year, start working now for next year's award.
You' ll find it well worth your while.
Unfortunately, one of the sad statistics that became apparent from a
review of the applications that were received, is that many of our Lodges

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

are neglecting our Masonic Affiliated Youth Groups in their activities.
These young people will all too soon be the leaders of our society and we
have a Masonic responsibility to see that they have the support and the
character development that they need while they are growing up. My
Brethren , we must take the time to provide this support.
The major functio n of the Lodge Resources Development Committee
is to assist Lodges in resolving problems that they may ha ve. Proble ms
can range from not knowing how to plan an activity to being unable to
o btain new officers. Ma ny times we find that the Brethren arc willing to
pitch in and do the work , but just don' t know how. Often they don't have
ideas for programs they can put on or they don't know how to plan and
carry them to execution. The Lodge Resources Development Committee
can help your Lodge overcome these obstacles. Our Committeeme n have
the background to work with you, and to help you to deve lop your own
program ideas. Tl1e Committee is presently working with ten ( 10) Lodges.
There are no overnight solutions, but results can be positive . How about
you? Wouldn't your Lodge benefit from some help in revitalizing your
programs?
We would like to take this opportunity to thank the Grand Secretary,
Very Worshipful Bob Klinger, and his staff for all of the help that they
have given us this past year.

During this past year it has been particularly gratifying to note the ever
increasi ng number of Lodges honoring the wives of departed Brothers. In
addition to the awarding of the Pins, various fo rms of recognition and
entertainment have featured activities in Lodges throughout the Jurisdiction .
Credit should be given to the dedication of the members of the Committee for their diligence in maintaining contact with their respective assignme nts.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
OLD MASONIC HALL AT LOS ANGELES
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A. M. of California:
A freshly-painted-and-decorated Old Masonic Hall at Los Angeles
greeted visitors from out-of-state and foreign countries that converged in
Los Angeles for the Olympiad Games.
Visitors to the refurbished Shrine of Masonry in Southern California
totaled approximately 2, l 00 for the year ending August 1984.
The painting of the structure in the Pueblo de Los Angeles, oldest street
in the City of Angels, was the first time in nearly 10 years . T he symbolic
frate rnal colors of shades of blue adorn the building, outdoors and indoors.
The recently installed air conditioning unit has proven a solid convenience in supplying comfort to visitors in the 60-seat Temple.
The old Temple is being glorified by two well-known local historians.
Dr. Judson G renie r, Professor of History, Cal State Dominquez, has spent

200

PROCEE DINGS OF THE

nearly a month looking at all the artifacts and ancient registers at the Hall .
He has photograp hed many objects and transcribe d on film innume rable
pages of historical records and lore. He is planning to write a histo rical
record of Freemaso nry in this area, based on facts and records at the first
home of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42 which received its charter in 1854.
Dr. Leonard Pitt , Ph. D., a historical consultant , is also writing an
analytical review of the Old Temple and the other buildings situated in
the Pico-Garn ier Block. He is doing this research for the old Los Angeles
Company which purchased the extensive real estate parcels and will develop them in the near future. He is pa rticularly interested in the negotiations with the State ;rnd the rehabilitation pla ns that were developed .
Both historians plan to present to Grand Lodge a nd our Old Temple
copies of their published work.
Twelve Lodges rented the Temple during the year for special degrees.
Three Masonic youth organizati ons presented their work during 1984.
Several reservatio ns are already booked for the 1984- 85 season.
(n January and May we circulated two mailings to Lodges in the lnspectoral Division letting these Masonic groups know of the availability
of renting the Temple for special meetings. and visiting the Temple at
416 1/2 North Main Street, in the north e nd of the downtown section . The
Temple is ope n to visitors o n Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday
from 10:00 A .M. to 3:00 P.M. Masonic Lodges pay a rental fee of $45.00
per night. Masonic youth groups are charged $25 .00 fo r a Saturday morn, ing degree date.
We have one permanen t tenant, Plaza de Los Angeles Lodge No. 814
which meets every Tuesday night.
Reservatio ns can be made by contacting the Chairman or the Custodian .
Brothe r Oliver Celaya , at 716 Traction Ave., Los Angeles. California
90013.
Distinctive degrees are presented to each group "working" at the Hall.
T hese can be framed as testament of having visited the Old Temple. We
expect 1984-85 to be ano ther banner year.
We believe that more Brethren should get acquainted with our Old
Temple. Plans are on the drawing board to conduct another direct ma iling
to Lodges in the area, as we ll as to concordan t Masonic groups.
Grey Line Buses. winding their way in the area , point out the Old
Masonic Hall to passengers on board . It has a lso appeared in three TV
specials created for the Olympics and restoration of the Pueblo de Los
Angeles sector. A picture of the Temple also appeared on the front cover
of the Telephone book for 1983- 84.
Respectfully submitted ,
MORRIS C. Guss, Chairman

REPOR T OF COMMI TTEE
ON MASONIC INFORMATION AND RESPON SIBILIT Y
To The Most Worshipfu l G rand L odge, F & A. M. of California:
During the several months prior to the Grand Lodge Communi cation
in October of 1983, the then progressiv e elective line held meetings with
committee chairmen in order to outline the projected program fo r the
coming Masonic year. Go als and objectives were promulgat ed for each
committee and our committee was charged with the following:
Objective : To assist the G rand Lodge and constitute d Lodges in promoting
Masonic education and understand ing as o utlined in Section
1234 C.M.C.
Goals: 1. Assure proper distributio n and recognitio n o f available published info rmation for Lodges and for public exposure .
2. Improve the e ffective ness of candidate investigati on, orie ntation and coaching.
3. Explain more meaningfu lly the history and philosophy of the 3
degrees to the new Masons progressin g through the 3 degrees.
4. Reduce the backlog of 1st, 2nd and 3rd degree proficienc ies
from 18% to 10% by year end 1984.
5. Excha nge and communicate with other appropria te Grand
Lodge Committe es the problem areas discovered withi n constituted Lodges.
To carry out this assignmen t and achieve our goals, it was felt that
working with and ,through the Masonic District Inspectors , and officers
and coaches of the vario us lodges assigned to those districts that much
could be accomplis hed in fulfilling our committee assignment.
According ly, each of o ur committee men was assigned several districts
and each was charged with the responsibi lity of actively visiting those
districts assigned and there to encourage the officers and members of the
several lodges there asse mb led t o sc hedule programs and mee tings
wherein committee men could participate and join in spreading the word
of Masonic Info rmation to our me mbers and the ir friends. ·
The Inspectors were most cooperative a nd he lpful in welcoming our
commitec men to their District schools of instruction , and for which courtesy o ur committee is most appreciati ve and grateful.
Our committee men , however, have not had equal success in securing
vast numbers of invitations from the officers of those districts to appear
at thei r lodges and to present our programs of Maso nic Info rmation at
their lodge meetings.
We have secured seven display boards fo r use by our committee men.
These were prepared and assembled by our for mer chai rman, Worshipful
Wayne C. Bates. For this service and his continuing support for our committee and its work, I wish to express my sincere appreciati on and tha nks
and that of each member of our committee .

REPORT OF THE MASONIC HISTORY COMMITTEE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Masonic History has been engaged this past year in
the continuation of the compilation of histories of the constituent Lodges.
Some of these histories have been condensed for inclusion in the California Freemason. The Winter 1983 issue featured histories of Nicolaus
Lodge No. 129, Sincerity Lodge No. 132 and Vacaville Lodge No. 134,
all celebrating 125th anniversaries. The Spring 1984 issue f~atured brief
histories of Anchor Lodge No. 273, celebrating its lOOth anniversary, and
Glendora Lodge No. 404 and Moneta Lodge No. 405, both celebrating
75th anniversaries. The Summer 1984 issue h ad the history of Brawley
Lodge No. 402 which celebrated its 75th anniversary. The Fall 1984 issue
had the history of Lebanon-Pacific Lodge No. 136 in honor of its 125th
anniversary.
The History Committee also prepared articles for the California Freemason on Masonry in California 125 and 100 years ago. These appeared
in the Summer and Fall issues respectively.

Worshipful E. Arthur Haglund reappointed all five members of th~ Omtman Masonic Temple Committee: William H. Lambert (13) , Chairman;
