The Committee met four times the past year, reviewing our past efforts
and discussing at length means for making the Library and Museum as
meaningful and as effective as possible. To that end we have concluded

210

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

that we need an inventory of our holdings and an appraisal made of our
Museum artifacts as well as our rare books for insurance purposes as well
as for accurately recording what we. do in fact have in our possession.
The Library receives numerous requests for duplicate titles but until our
holdings have been gone over, book by book, no list can be sent out until
such a list is made. We have some 12,000 volumes; 3,000 have been catalogued of which but 600 have been accurately carded and cross filed as
to title , author and subject.
The Museum contains some 2,500 items ; most have been recorded but
no attempt has been made to cross index as to type of item or donor. At
best, just a sketch or written description has had to suffice in describing
the numerous rare and expensive items. We hope for adequate funds to
appraise and photograph the more valuable items for our insurance records to ascertain how many of what kind of item we have as well as for
aiding in recovery of same in case of loss.
. We have in our drawers , hundreds of photographs and prints, slides ,
films , newspapers, periodicals and images or documents of historic Masonic events, cornerstone layings, parades, important and not so important
Masonic figures, Temples-all yet to be sorted , recorded and made conveniently available to our members.
Cassette tapes and oral history-with the decline of letter writing and
the keeping of diaries , sources of Masonic history by eyewitnesses or participants will soon become lost. We have several taped Lodge histories as
well as 40 or more Maso nic lectures and addresses by prominent Masonic
speakers on a variety of topics. Means must be found to inform the membership of this valuable tool. We have numerous Research Lodge publications in depth-no cross filing, little indexing. We have quite good Genealogical research materials; no indexing.
The Committee has concluded that the Library and Museum desperately
need the steady employment of a library technician who views record
keeping as an end in itself and who would not only take care of the daily
tasks but with the help of the volunteer staff eventually accurately record
our holdings so that we know what we have in our possession.
Our budget request for the ensuing year is in the amount of $15,000.00,
of which $7 ,500.00 is for employment of a technician, and the remainder
for staff expense as well as usual Library expenses of acquisitions , dues,
postage.
We are also asking for a supplemental request of $3 ,000.00 to defray
the travel expenses, in part, in appraising our Museum artifacts as well as
for film and other unanticipated costs incidental thereto.
The Library and Museum are open five days a week from 10:00 A.M.
to 3:00 P.M. and by request as needed. We again ask special commendation
and encouragement to the loyal and dedicated corps of volunteers who
chee rfully assist visitors and painstakingly do all the details necessary to
operate the Library and Museum. They are Brothers Larry West, Jack
Taylor, George Walda, LeRoy Bilsborough , Haig Soghomonian, Thomas
Storer, Louis Wells, Joseph Friedman, Ironton Dau be. Bernie Katz, Joel
Yager, David Shull and Harold Ecklund.

We arc grateful for the cooperation and enthusiastic support of Grand
Secretary Robert A. Klinger and the capable office staff who so cheerfully
respond to all our needs and requests , and to Loren Stritenberger, General
Manager, and the staff of the California Masonic Memorial Temple for
their graciously offered assistance when needed. Finally, we desire to express sincere appreciation a nd thanks to our Grand Master, Most Worshipful E. Arthur Haglund, for his loyal support and encouragement.

Following the Youth Breakfast at the Fairmont Hotel the Brethren and
their ladies formed in procession and paraded along California Street to
the California Masonic Memorial Temple Auditorium led by representatives from the Inttrnational Order of DeMolay, International Order of
Job's Daughters and the International Order of Rainbow for Girls. Whe n
all were seated in the Auditorium , a recently produced film concerning
the Statue of Liberty Restoration Project, introduced by Past Master
Royal Dano , was viewed. At the conclusion of this film the Grand Lodge
Officers entered the Auditorium and assumed their stations. The Invocation was delivered by the Very Reverend Sargent J. Wright , Grand
Chaplain.
The Representatives of o ur Youth Groups marched into the Auditorium, each one carrying an American Flag. All joined in the singing of
our National Anthem, led by the Grand Orator, Donald A. Nielsen. The
Grand Marshal escorted eight Youth Leaders into the Auditorium and
placed the m West of the altar where he individually introduced the young
dignitaries. The Grand Maste r personally welcomed each of the young
people and invited them to take seats in the East.
The Grand Marshal retired and escorted the dignitaries representing
the Concordant and Appendant Bodies of Masonry in California into the
Grand Lodge. They, too, were individually introduced by the Grand Marshal and cordially welcomed by the Grand Master and escorted to seats
provided for them.

To these basic "plays" we added others called tenets - Brotherly Love
and Relief. To succeed as a strong team we must aid, support and protect
each other.
Our Youth Groups are crying for our aid and support. They need us as
advisors and active participants in their activities. Yet every year more
and more Bethels, Assemblies and Chapters relinquish their charters because there is no interest on the part of adults. We are supposed to be
men of vision, but I fear our sight is growing dim when it comes to the

215

"No nation, and especially not this one at this stage
in its history, can afford to neglect its children.
Whatever importance we attach as people to expenditure
on armaments, to programs for older Americans, to
maintaining high levels of consumption and to a hundred
other purposes, the welfare of the children has to be
our highest priority. Not only are they our future
security, but their dreams and ideals can provide a
much-needed renaissance of spirit in what is becoming
an aging, tired , and disillusioned society. In the
end , the only thing we have is our young people; if we
fail them , all else is in vain."
Former President Dwight D. Eisenhower put our dedication to youth
through our support of public schools this way,
"Because our schools help shape the mind and character
of our youth, the strength or weakness of our
educational system today will go far to determine the
strength or weakness of our national wisdom and our
national morality tomorrow. That is why it is
essential to our nation that we have good schools and
their quality depends on all of us."
Horace Mann , the founder of public education wrote,
" Remember the child . Pour out light and truth as God
pours sunshine and rain . No longer seek knowledge as
the luxury of a few, but dispense it amongst all as the
bread of life. Summon the mightiest intellects.
Collect whatever talent or erudition or eloquence the
broad land can supply, and go forth and teach this
people."
Well, this season is over. We've reviewed many of our " plays". Now it's
time for each of you to evaluate yo urself.
Suppose every Maso n did what you did?
Suppose every Mason attended meetings with the regularity
you do?

Suppose every Mason served on as many Committees as you
do?
Suppose every Mason brought in as many petitions as you do?
Suppose every Mason was as friendly, thoughtful and considerate as you are?
Suppose every Mason was as dependable , conscientious, enthusiastic and willing as you are?
Suppose every Mason had as many, or few excuses as you do?
Suppose every Mason followed your example?
What kind of a Fraternity would we have?
As for me there is only one answer. It can be great, it must be

REPORT OF MASONIC
LEADERSHIP WORKSHOP COMMITTEE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A. M. of California:
Important changes were made in the structure of this Committee to
provide that it would no longer be limited to Senior and Junior Wardens.
but would be available to all officers and interested sidcliners in all
Lodges. Most Worshipful E. Arthur Haglund, Grand Master, took a personal interest in the plans for the year's operations, and in accordance
with those plans, seven Workshops were held in Cities throughout California, plus one in the State of Hawaii.
Most of the Workshops ran from 10:00 A.M. until 3:30 P.M. with a
break of an hour and one-half at lunch, when the Executive Committee
usually in full force addressed the entire gathering and answered questions
which were propounded. During classroom sessions, the entire crowd was
divided into three separate classes running simultaneously, and each
taught by a different instructor, a Brother selected for his experience in
Masonry and for his ability as a speaker and leader of discussion.
A nominal charge was made for registration and for lunch which was
prepared by the Host Lodge or other Body. General approval was received
from those in ~ttendance, and a rather detailed record was kept of their
comments. Most of those who attended recommended that the Workshops
be continued and that the general format be used in future years.
Instructors were generally drawn from members of the Workshop Committee, but occasionally one was invited outside of the Committee. The
Grand Secretary provided extremely useful service in arranging for meeting places and for taking reservations. The principal promotion for the
meetings was made through the Inspectors and without their support, very
little could be accomplished. lt is recomme nded that the Workshops be
continued either in the same format or with such improvements as can be
devised .
Respectfully submitted,
EVERETT HousER, Chairman

The Public Information Committee participated in this year's series of
state-wide workshops. For most participants in these workshops, this was
the first time that the topic of public relations had been presented and
discussed. While we found that many Lodges do carry out an active public
relations program, most Lodges do not make use of this important promotional tool. In these workshops, we concentrated o n showing effective
ways that the publicity kit can be used on the local level.
On specialized occasions during the year, the public Informatio n Committee has sent "sample" news releases to Lodges for their submission to
news editors in their areas. These news releases were written so they could
easily be changed and adapted for Lodge use. One of the news release
topics related to the spring TV mini-series on George Washington. Other
topics included the Statue of Liberty restoration project and Lodge donatio ns to the Masonic Ho mes.
This past year, we also have developed a public relations program for
the California Masonic Foundation . News releases have been written and
disseminated to news editors of local papers where the scholarship prese ntations have taken place.
The Public Information Committee members also have been wor king
either on a one-on-one or small grou p level with Lodge publicity chairmen

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
The Grand Lodge Committee on Taxation advises o n matters of taxation
at the request of the Grand Lodge , subordinate Lodges anq other o rganizations under their jurisdiction. We have advised on matters of income.
property. sales, employment, estate and gift tax matters. In this annual
report. we have historically discussed items of current interest in the taxation of fraternal organizations.
This Committee is frequently asked to comment on the tax exempt
status of Temple Associations. In order to be exempt from the payme nt

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GR AND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

o f Federal and California taxes on the net income o f a Temple Association .
wholly owned by a Lodge , the exclusive business of the Temple Association must be to hold title to property, collect income from the prope rty
and annually turn over the e ntire amount o f such income, less expenses ,
to the Lodge which owns it. Internal Reve nue Code Sections SOl(a),
501(c)(2), (10). California Revenue and Taxation Code Section 23701h.
The articles of incorpo ration for a Temple Association should include this
•
exclusive purpose .
In determining the amount of net income which must be turned over
to the Lodge , any expense incurred by the Temple Association reduces
the amount of income required to be remitted to the Lodge. The te rm
"expense" includes not only out-of-pocket expenditures but also reaso nable additions to depreciation reserves. Sec Rev. Rul. 66-102 , 1966-1 C. B .
133, R ev. Rul. 67-104, 1967-1 C.B. 120. Because of possibly differing
interpre tations of what is reasonable, this Committee recomme nds that a
Te mple Association turn over its entire net cash profit for the year to the
Lodge which owns it . If the Temple Association in future years requires
additional cash, the Lodge can then return the money to the Temple Association. Of course, any reinvestment of funds in the Temple Association
should not be done without obtaining the consent of the Grand Lodge
Committee on Temple Properties. California Masonic Code Section 2304.
Should the property owned by the Temple Association be sold subsequently, the net income distribution rule would require the Temple Association to dissolve and transfer its remaining assets to the Lodge.
The Internal Revenue Service has officially recognized that the Grand
Lodge of California and its subordinate Lodges are exempt from income
tax under Internal Revenue Code Section 50 l(c)(10), regardless of the
amount of income received from dues or o n bank accounts or other investments. It is Group Exemption No. 0214, memorialized in a lette r dated
July 11 , 1972 from the l.R.S. to the Grand Lodge, which letter had the
following identification code: T:MS:EO:R: I. However, the Grand. L?dge
does not ma intain a group exemption for individual Temple Assoc1at1ons.
Application for recognition of exempt status sho uld be made to the I. R.S.
on Form 1024 and to the State of California on FTB 3500. Detailed instructio ns are published with these forms regarding their proper completion. If a Temple Association is entitled to e xe mpt status, its income is
exempt from tax even if derived from commerical tenants and therefore
not just Masonic organizations .
Some of our Temple A ssociations have found that they have never applied for exempt status. Without applying for recognitio_n ?f such ~talu s,
the government may attempt to tax the Temple Assoc1at10n on its net
income for the year. If a Te mple Associatio n finds that its exempt status
is questioned , a member of the Committee should be contacted. (It sho~ld
be noted that the Postal Service is investigating more closely persons usmg
the special third-class bulk rate available to nonprofit , fraternal o rganizations. In some areas, the Postal Service has required proof of exempt
status before granting or continuing a right to mail at the specia l thirdclass bulk rate.)

Temple Associations have the same tax return filing requirements with
the Internal Revenue Service and the California Franchise Tax Boa rd as
do Lodges. They are required to file Federal Form 990 and California
Form 199 for a ny taxa ble year in which gross receipts are in excess of
$25 ,000. Temple A ssociations with annual gross receipts of $25,000 or less
are required only to file California Form 1998.
Temple Associations are not exempt from any other taxes such as Calif<:>rnia sale and use taxes or property taxes. or from the requirement to
withhold and pay employment taxes wi th respect to employees.
While a Masonic Lodge is not taxable on its income from dues and
investments. it is not the type of o rganization which can receive gifts which
are ded uctible for income, gift or estate tax purposes unless the funds are
transferred to the Lodge with the express request that they be redirected
to a charity which is qualified to receive such tax deductible contributions ,
such as the Masonic Homes of California. Section 170(c )( 4) of the Internal
Revenue . Code of I 954. Also, contributions to a Temple Association for
its ex~lus_ivc use arc not deductible for income, gift or estate tax purposes.
Penod1cally, Lodges and individuals a re asked for proof that contributio ns to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund are deductible for income
g~ft or estate tax purposes. California Masonic Code Section 1406b pro~
v1des that the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund is an asset of the Masonic
Homes of California. The Masonic Ho mes of California is listed as an
l.R.C. Section 50 l(c)(3) organization in Publication 78 (Rev. 1-84), Cumulative List of Organizations described in Section 170(c) of the Internal
Revenue Code of 1954. This publication together with the California Mason~c Code should be sufficient evidence of the exempt status of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund and sufficient evidence that contributions
!o .su~h .Fund are dCductible for income, gift and estate tax purposes. Even
1f md1v1duals make such contributions through Lodges, the contributions
arc still deductible if given to the Lodge with specific instructions that the
contributions be forwarded by the Lodge to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund .
Recently, ma ny Lodges were advised by the Internal Revenue Service
and the State of California that certain payments made by Lodges and
Temple Associations totalling $600 o r more during a calendar year must
be reported to the Inte rna l Reve nue Service on Form 1099 and the Franchise .Tax Boa_rd on Form 599 prior to Ma rch 1st of the following year.
Such. mformat1on re turns are required for payments in the form of wages,
salanes, rent. premiums, annuities , compe nsation, remuneration or otherwise in a mo unts of $600 or mo re in a single calendar yea r. If the payments are dividends or interest , the dollar threshold for reporting is reduced to $10 a year. No such reporting is required for payments made to
an employee whose wages are prope rl y reported on Form W-2. Failure to
c?~ply with these. rules could subject the paying Lodge or Temple A ssoe1at1on to a $50 fme from the Inte rnal Revenue Service a nd a $10 fine
from the State of Califo rnia for each failure to file. It should be noted
that a Form 1099 and a Form 599 need not be filed if the payee is a

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON YOUTH ORDERS
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A. M. of California:
Your Committee un Youth Orders has been active this year in a continued effort to support and promote the health and general welfare of our
Masonic Youth Groups.
As has been the case for the last number of years, our Masonic Youth
Orders continue to grow smaller in terms of net membership. However,
that trend in membership loss has slowed and there is some encouragement
that the "turning of the corner" or at least a leveling off of membership
may be in sight. In spite of a decline in total membership, the Masonic
Youth Organizations in California and Hawaii continue to be vigorous,
active and healthy and to be extremely well thought of nationally in their
respective organizations.
The primary concerns of this Committee with regard to the relationship
between the California Grand Lodge and the various youth organizations
continues to center around the lack of understa nding on the part of our
Lodges and our Masons as to who the youth organizations are and how
they fit into the Masonic family. As a corollary to this, the youth organizations continue to need a larger number of qualified, dedicated adult
leaders to support the youth in their organizations and activities. This is
not to say that there arc not many outstanding examples of superior relationships between Lodges and local Assemblies, Bcthels and Chapters.
Nevertheless. we continue to learn of gross examples of misundersta nding
and little or no Masonic support in certain localities.
On August 19, 1984 a meeting was held under the auspices of this
Committee between the Executive Committee of the Grand Lodge and
the various adult Heads of Youth Orders in California. The major items
of discussion were as follow:
A. Timely, co mplete and more frequent communications between the
youth orders themselves and between various youth orders and
Grand Lodge needs to be promoted and improved. This can take
the form of better coordination between the groups as to the ir activities and the cross-participation in them , the exchange of calen-

IMPLEMENTATION OF

1983 GRAND MASTER'S RECOMMENDATION NO. 3
OPTIONAL USE OF A
" SHORT FORM" CLOSING CEREMONY

225

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
At the 1983 Annual Communication, the n G rand Master H arry L.
Maynard recommended that the Ritual Committee develop a " Short
Form" Closing Ceremony to be used by the Constituent Lodges as an
optional method of closing Lodges at all special meetings.
First , let's take a look at what this might do for the Lodges. The savings
in time would represent approximately four minutes in the first Degree,
three minutes in the Second Degree , and six and one half minutes in the
Third Degree-hardly an appreciable gain when compared to a lifetime
commitme nt to Freemasonry. This same time gai n can be realized by
simply adjusting the starting time of special meetings. Our ritual is like
a n old building. It is only a comparatively small part of the total community. However, it is a link with our past a nd a part of our heritage.
Once it is to rn down it is gone foreve r and eventually it is not even a
memory. Let us think very carefully before we do this to even a small
part of our ritual and heritage of our Craft.
Secondly, your Committee has consistently relied upo n Section 2690
C.M.C., which says in pa rt : "The G rand Lodge alone has power to autho rize any changes in the ritual for the purpose of having it remain as it
was handed down from time immemorial." The Ritual Committee relied
upon this same concept in 1983, when they recommended that the First
Degree Lecture be 'returned to its original form.
We find evidence as far back as 1852 where Grand Masters have demanded that Lodges must be closed. We do no t , however, find any other
form of closing than the one we now use.
The question can be raised : " How then can the Grand Master use a
sho rt form in closing the Grand Lodge?" That is a good question. Section
1000 C. M.C. states, 'The Grand Mas ter possesses o nly those powers contained in the Constitution a nd Ordinances of this Grand Lodge and those
expressly de legated to him by his Brethren." In the absence of expressed
autho rity in this specific case, we must re ly upon Section 1032 of the Code
which grants certain discretionary powe rs to the Grand Master. If this
aut hority is to be followed, then such powe r must remain in , ·and with,
the station of the Grand Master, and cannot be transmitted to the Master
of a Lodge.
Absent a change in Section 2690, we believe that we are obligated to
vote " No" on this proposal , and your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes so recommends .

The Commirtee on Ritual:

Temple Association (or similar e ntity in which it has an ownership interest)
from losses resulting from poor business practices such as failure to insure
or to under-insure . and such facts should he taken into consideration in
considering applications for relief.
6. Consideration should be given to allowing the fund to be capable of
receiving gifts and loans from Masonic Lodges as well as individual members of the Craft, and legislation should be drafted to accomplish this
purpose , if required.
7. The study and report should consider whe ther there should be emergent or long-term relief, or both; the size of the fund; the limit of relief
in any given case; and, the method of creating the Fund.
8. The Fund must be wholly discretionary with the ultimate authority
and responsibility for its administration in the Grand Master.

We found that the Coastside loss was one which could have been (but
was not) insured against and we we re unable to discove r any other losses
during the last 15 years which could not have been relieved by adequate
insurance.
It became apparent that , although long-term loss could be cared for by
adequate insurance, the re was a demonstrated need in many cases for
emergent assistance to protect prope rty, provide alternate accommodatio ns , and the like. It was the failure to provide a fund for replacement
of o lder buildings, and the omission of adequate insurance which turned
an unfortunate loss into a disaster in many cases.
Al though it was concluded that the assets of the Grand Lodge. which
primarily result from the per capita assessment of the members, should
not be used to substitute for the good business practice of insuring against
disasters, it was felt that the cost of such insurance , particularly in hi gh
risk a reas subject to earthquake, flood , landslide, subsidence, tidal wave
damage and the like might well have created a practical impossibility of
providing the necessary protection. For this reason, through the splendid
efforts of the Insurance Committee with the cooperation of Thompkins &
Company, a plan known as "DIFFERENCE IN CONDITIONS INS U RANCE" has been made available at a cost of approximately $3.00 per
thousand of insurance . In cooperation with the Temple Properties Committee, the Insurance Committee is making a survey of the Temple Associations to determine whethe r the re is an interest in providing such
coverage. It is intended tha t the policy will cover the major exclusions
with which we are concerned ; namely, earthquake, flood, landslide , subsidence, and tidal wave damage.
Having found that insurance at a reasonable cost is available to pay
losses resulting frnm disasters , your Committee concluded that it could
not recommend to this Grand Lodge that it should provide Jong-term rel ief
to those Lodges which elected not to purchase insurance. To do so would
be asking all Masons to co ntribute their monies to a large fund which
would be required to care for those who , having the ability to do so, failed
to care for themselves. We did conclude, however, that a fund of reasonable size is necessary and desirable to assist o ur Lodges on an emergent
or short-term basis in the case of disasters.
This Committee concluded that the following should he used as guidelines in the creation of a short-term disaster relie f fund :

228

The Committee members proceeded to inte rview representatives of
Lodges which recently had suffered disasters such as Coastside No. 762
and Coalinga No. 387 to determine the nature and exte nt of their losses
and how a Fund , if created, could have been of assistance. Worshipful
Brother Frank Cox of Kauai Lodge No. 589 was interviewed by telephone ,
at which time it was learned that although two members of that Lodge
suffered perso nal losses from Hurricane Eva, the Temple fortunately was
unscathed.
Grand Secretary Robert A. Klinger was most helpful in supplying statistical information as was Brother Jay Newman, the President of Thompkins & Company Insurance Brokers, which firm has long serviced a substantial portion of Grand Lodge, Masonic Homes , and constituent Lodge
insurance.
The Committee called upon State and Federal Disaster Relief agencies
and the American Red Cross to determine the ir criteria for relief, and
communicated by telephone with Very Worshipful Brother Frank Arnold.
the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge A. F. & A . M. of Missouri. to
acquaint ourselves with the scope of their Disaster Relief Fund.
We learned from Taxation Chairman Doan that the Fund would not
qualify for tax deductible contributions. as the entities to receive the benefits are not themselves charities .
In looking historically at the need of our Grand Lodge for a Disaster
Relief Fund, we found that the Coalinga earthquake loss was substantially
covered by insurance notwithstanding the fact that such insurance had not
specifically been purchased. This was due to the fortuity of certain recent
California litigation which cast doubt upon the effectiveness of the earthquake exclusion in the policy as it then read . Such coverage could, however, have been purchased.

1. The fund should be available only for the emergent relief of disasters.
These funds should be available to prevent further loss; to provide temporary quarters; and to allow the Lodge to continue to function for a
limited pe riod until destroyed properties can be repaired or replaced or
alternative solutions are reached by the Lodge.
2. The Grand Maste r shall have ultimate authority and discre tion to
determine whether the occurrence is eligible to be considered as a disaster.
the amount and duration of relief. and whethe r the relief should be in the
form of a gift or a loan.
3. The fund. if created. shall not have retroactive applicability.

4. The fund should be created by a 5-cent per capita assessment per
year for a term of five years or until the fund, including earnings, has
attained an amount over $50,000.00 but less than $60,000.00.
5. Should the fund at any time after attaining at least $50,000.00 drop
below that amount , the 5-cent per year per capita assessment shall automatically be reinstated until the fund again exceeds $50,000.00 but is less
than $60,000.00.
6. It should not be the intention to allow the fund to grow interminably
and, therefore, when the fund attains $100,000.00 all earnings over that
limit shall be paid over to the general fund of the Grand Lodge.

GRAND LODGE DISASTER RELIEF FUND
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

RESOLVED that Section 1810 be added to the California Masonic
Code to read as follows:
1810. DISASTER RELIEF FUND. A disaster relief fund administered
by or under the direction of the Grand Master shall be available to provide
emergent and short-term relief to constituent Lodges which suffer property losses from disasters. The purpose of the fund is to provide monies
to be used to prevent further loss; to provide temporary Lodge facilities;
and/or to allow the Lodge to continue to function for a limited period
until destroyed property can be repaired or replaced or alternative remedies completed.
"The monies shall be made available to the Lodge in the form of a grant
or a loan, and in amounts and for terms as determined by the Grand
Master.
"Until such time as the Fund has a corpus of at least $50 ,000.00, but
no more than $60,000.00, there shall be assessed five cents per capita per
year to create the fund. Should the fund at any time fall below $50,000.00,
the five cents per capita per year assessment shall be reinstated until the
fund is restored to a corpus of at least $50,000.00, but no more than
$60,000.00.
"Should the corpus of the fund attain $100,000.00, all accumulations
thereafte r from earnings or otherwise shall be paid over to the General
Fund of the Grand Lodge."
FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 350 be amended by deleting the
word 'and' after the semi-colon in sub-paragraph 3rd thereof; by substituting a semi-colon for the period at the end of sub-paragraph 4th thereof;
and adding the word 'and' thereto; and adding sub-paragraph 5th as follows :

(1)
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to permit, if a candidate for
degrees so requests, the use of H oly Writings other than the Holy Bible
as one of the principal furnishings of a regula r Lodge .

.

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of Californ ia:
WHEREAS , God is one, but He is called by different names; and
WHEREAS , Masonry is universal and unites men of every natio n, sect,
a nd opinion; and
WHEREAS, the belief in the Supreme Being varies among the human
race, and the volume of sacred law is different among various religions;
a nd
WHEREAS , at present only the Holy Bible is one of the furnishings
of every legal Lodge , instead of the Holy Writings of all other major
religions; and
WHEREAS, this discriminatory process may be preventing prospective
Bro thers, with non-Christian beliefs, from joining our Fraternity.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that one of the principal
furnishings of a regular Lodge will remain the Holy Bible , but the Ho ly
Writings of other major religions. such as the Torah or Koran , may be
used if a candidate so desires it.
RESOLVED FURTHER, that the Ritual Committee shall amend all
ritual and publications of the Gra nd Lodge as necessary to carry out the
intent of this Resolution.

".our Comm_ittee therefore submits no legislation. hut proposes the following resolutmn:
. RESOIYED that on~ of the principal furnishings at a regular Lodge

Our ritual clearly does not inte nd that use of the Holy Bible demands,
or even suggests , that a candidate compromise his own religious beliefs,
nor is it intended to require that he adopt or recognize an y part of the
Christian religion.
The Ho ly Bible adorns our Sacred Altar as an inspirational symbol upon
which all men with a belief in a Supreme Being can agree, a nd upon which
me n of all faiths may receive and accept a solemn vow with the highest
degree of sincerity. One of the distinguishing features of the Grand Lodge
of California has been a strong impulse toward unanimity.
Adoption of this Resolution would require changes in our ritual of major
proportions, in that the words " Holy Bible" a re used 23 times in the
degrees and candidates lectures now taught by the Grand Lecturer of this
Grand Lodge. Sectio n 2690 C.M.C. states in part that. "The Grand Lodge
alone has a power to authorize any changes in the ritual for the purpose
of having it remain as it was handed down fro m time immemorial." H istorically, construction of this Section, by the Grand Lodge, has limited
even the broad powers of the Grand Lodge to that of preserving the ritual
as originally adopted. Rituals of Ceremony, howe ver, arc not bound by
this Section .
Freemasonry is not a religion. But we arc a brotherhood engaged in
moral teaching. The lectures of our three degrees are replete with those
moral teachings. gleaned from the pages of the Holy Bible, and our Officers Monitor contains five passages of scripture from the same so urce,
none of which are, or should be, repugnant to the sincere candidate for
Freemasonry.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a " No"
vote.

The Committee on Ritual:

Re~olution No. I proposes to "permit candidates for the degrees to
su~st1tute the Holy W;rttn~s of their choice, in place of the Holy Bible."
This marks the third time tn the last seven years that this issue has been
before the Grand Lodge.
. In 1976, on the recommendation of then Grand Master Roberts, a Special Com~1ttee was appointed to study this subject and report its reeo~mendat1ons at the 1977 Annual Communication. Included in the Committee report were statements from Masonic Authorities in the fi eld of
Theolog_y ~ho cited a myriad of prohlems that could arise if "the practice
of substituting other books for the Holy Bible in obligating a candidate"
was .adopted. The Special Committee recommended that the Holy Bible
eontmue to be the. only book upon which all candidates are obfigated.
That reco?1mendat1~n was adopted by the Grand Lodge.
Resolut10n No. 5. in 1979, again brought this proposal before the Grand
L?dge, an?, as before , it was th~ will of the Grand Lodge that the Holy
Bible contmue to be used_ exclusively. It is the opinion of your Policy and
General Purposes Committee that this policy should prevail in 1984.

At the Annual Communication of 1976 this Grand Lodge adopted the
Recomme ndation of John F. Roberts, Jr. to form a committee consisting
of the Policy and General Purposes Committee , the Jurisprudence Committee and the Ritual Committee . The sole purpose of this committee was
to determine what changes would be req uired to permit an obligation to
be taken on Holy Writings other than the Holy Bible.
That committee reported as follows: "In making this study ma ny factors
were considered by the committee , each having a strong bearing upon the
subject. The most important of these considerations, however, is t he great
number of changes in our law and ritual , and additional problems for
Lodges which would result from the substitution of another book for the
Holy Bible.
"Because of the complex nature of the study, the committee deemed it
advisable and necessary to seek additional advice of those more expert in
the field of Theology and Holy Writings. Opinions were therefore sol icited
from Brothers Roland A. Bach and R abbi Edgar Magnin , both former
Grand Chaplains and recognized authorities in the field of Theology.

AVAILABILITY OF WIDOW'S PIN TO ALL WIDOWS
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to amend •.he Monitor ~nd. Officers Manual by allowing the option to use abbreviated Masonic titles
when addressing mail.
.
The proponent states that the present instruction is not ncc~ssary.. since
titles are contained in Trcstleboards, which arc usually mailed without
envelopes, and presumably will be read . He further states that there docs
not appear in the California Masonic Code any regulation forhi.dding the
use of titles at such times, but that it is merely shown as an advisory note
in the Monitor and Officers Manual. In addition, the writer of this Resolution says that inclusion of the title would be an honor due to one who
has attained his present position through years of dedication, and that no
harm to the Grand Lodge or constituent Lodges would result if these titles
were used.
While it is true that most Trestleboards are mailed without an envelope,
the presence of abbreviated titles are meaningless to anyone but a Mason .
We can assume that the postman , in whose possession that Trestleboard
is for a longer period of time than in anyone else's, does not have either
the time or the inclination to try to fathom the meaning of the initials. If
he is not a Mason, the initials would mean nothing. If he is a Mason, he
may already know the addressee's title, so inclusion of the title is unneeded .
•
The purpose of the Resolution is presumably for the honor of the re• 1
cipicnt only. We feel that the attainment of a certain position in ~he Grand
Lodge or Constituent Lodges is indeed an honor, but that adding an abbreviation of his title to a piece of mail would not add to a man's self
esteem . We arc happy in the knowledge that we have attained some measure of status in Masonry. That is payment enough.

affiliation.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes"
vote . This Committee is authorized to report that the Masonic Widows
Com mittee concurs with our report and recomme nds a " Yes" vote .

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence , to which Resolution No . 4 has been
referre d , reports as follows :
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to establish a rotation plan for
the appointment of Grand Lodge Officers so as to insure that an Appointive Officer previously appointed may not be again appointed to any selected appointive offices, and, further, that appointments may not twice
be made from the same Lodge until all other Lodges have had a member
appointed as a Grand Lodge Officer.
To carry out the intent of the proponent, your Committee submits the
following legislation:
RESOLVED that Section 204 of the California Masonic Code be
amended by adding the following paragraphs:
"No Lodge with a member who has served as an Appointive Grand
Lodge Officer may have ;mother member appointed as such until all
Lodges which have not had a member so appointed. have had a member
receive such an appointment.
"The Grand Master shall not appoint a member who has previously
served as an Appointive Grand Lodge Officer in any of the following
office:
Grand Chaplain
Grand Orator
Grand Marshal
Grand Standard Bearer
Grand Sword Bearer
Grand Bible Bearer

Senior Grand Deacon
Junior Grand Deacon
Senior Grand Steward
Junior Grand Steward
Grand Pursuivant
Grand Tiler."

The proponent of Resolution No. 4 seeks to establish a rotation system
for the appointment of certain Grand Lodge Officers. It would appear, at
first glance , that nothing could be fairer or more Masonic. A closer look
at the ramifications of such a plan reveals that it is almost unworkable.
The key words in this issue are presented by the proponent himself in
the first sentence of the proposal: "The position of Grand Lodge Officer
is a highly respected and prestigious position ." It is for this very reason
that the incoming Grand Master should have the very broadest latitude
in selecting the Grand Lodge Officers who will carry the Masonic message
during his term of office.
Adoption of this Resolution would implement a rotation system
whereby each Lodge would receive a Grand Lodge Officer appointment
every 52 years . It does not, however, provide for the disparity that it would
create between our smallest Lodge of 38 members and our largest Lodge
of 1, 188 members . The small Lodge would receive one appointment for
every 1,976 member-years of the Lodge . while the large Lodge would
receive one appointment for every 61,776 member-years. Many Lodges
a re having difficulty finding Officers and Committeemen to run the affairs
of their own Lodge , and, thus, would not appear to be fertile grounds to
search for Grand Lodge Officers by mandate.
Ability, achievement and excellence comes always from the individual
and not from a collection of Lodge Numbers and Charters. It is from the
individual members that we must continue the selection process for those
who will represent the offices of our Grand Lodge.
Within the last five years two Grand Orators have been selected from
the same Lodge, not because of special privilege, but, rather, because
each of those Grand Masters saw in these two individuals an opportunity
to extend his own Masonic voice and philosophy. Under the proposed
system the second of these two members would have been well over a
hundred years old before becoming eligible for appointment, and as a
result his talents would have been lost to us.
The Resolution does not provide for an effective date for implementing
the proposed system, if adopted, and so we must assume that the incoming
Grand Master would have to search the rosters all the way back to 1850
in order to establish eligibility and be in compliance. We suggest that his
time could be better utilized in planning for the future.
The Committee agrees in part with the second paragraph of the Resolution and suggests that incoming Grand Masters avoid reappointment of
previous Grand Lodge Officers. We do not , however, recommend the
binding effect of making it a part of the la w.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No"
vote .
Not Adopted.

To place the matter before Grand Lodge , we move the adoption of the

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Each of Resolutions numbered 5 and 6 has the same goal, a definition
of the duties of the Standing Committee on United States Constitution
Observance. Each was referred to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes which makes this report.
Last year at its Annual Communication this Grand Lodge amended
Section 1202 of the Masonic Code to make the Committee on United
States Constitution Observance a Standing Committee. This was a recognition of the important and permanent nature of the work of this Committee. There now needs to be adopted a statement of the duties of that
Committee.
Masons have more than the usual reason to be proud of the United
States Constitution. Many of the delegates to the convention which drafted
the Constitution were Masons. Much of the language contained in the
Constitution has Masonic significance . These reasons, in addition to the
lasting quality of that inspired document, came as great pride in the instrument which created the rules by which we are governed.
One of the virtues of our Constitution is its brevity. By stating most
principles in broad terms, without great specificity the Constitution can
be, and has been, interpreted in different ways to meet the diffe rent needs
of different times.
This same principle causes us to favor Resolution 6. This Resolution is
not specific in stating the duties of the Committee. The problem with a
more detailed and specific definition of duties is that it limits the Committee. When duties are generally defined, the Committee can be as inge nious as imagination and money will allow.

248

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Thus. the Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a
"No" vote on Resolution Number 5 and a "Yes" vote on Resolution Number 6.

The Committee on United States Constitution Observance:
As has been stated, legislation was adopted at the 1982 Grand Lodge
Communication which changed the status of this Committee from that of
a "Special Committee'' to that of a "Standing Committee." That piece of
legislatio n did not provide for the duties of the Committee, and since the
California Masonic Code has heretofore outlined the duties for all "Standing" Committees, Resolution No. 5 and Resolution No. 6 were submitted
to establish such duties.
To preve nt any misunderstanding, perhaps I should interject at this
point that even without specific and codified duties, this Grand Lodge has
no t had an inactive Constitution Observance Committee for the past two
years; quite the contrary, I assure you!
The real problem at this moment is the selection of the Resolution which
will be the most appropriate , and since both are appare ntly legally correct,
it becomes your province to choose between the two.
It is our opinion that the proper choice sho uld be Resolution No. 6.
This o pinion is based upon the following:
Resolution No. 5 seeks to enact a number of "specific" type duties for
the Committee which may, over the long term become restrictive and
limiting, not only to the Committee but also may very well pre-empt the
authority, the desire , and the imagination of the Masters of the Constituent
Lodges. We do not believe that this Committee sho uld ever be restrained
in any way in its efforts to assist Lodges in their preparations of meaningful
observances. Nor should the Lodges be limited in planning programs best
suited for their capacity or their needs.
It is our further opinion that Resolution No. 6 adequately provides the
measures necessary to insure the proper functions of this Grand Lodge
Committee. It is a well worded Resolution and does not embody the
specific a nd restricted measures found in Resolution No. 5.
To sum up, it is our contention that the broad la nguage of Resolutio n
No. 6 will best serve the interests a nd the goals of the G rand Lodge, and
will not in any way limit the extent of efforts by future committees. We
recommend a "No" vote on Resolutio n No. 5 and recommend a "Yes"
vote on Resolution No. 6.
Adopted.

It is not clear why the wording. "when requested by his family," was
added since it was not included in the Grand Master's Recommendation.
In 1969 a Resolution was introduced which would have permitted
Lodges to make donations to any group or organization as designated by
a deceased Brother's family. The Resolution was not adopted. The Policy
& General Purposes Committee kit that Lodge funds should not include
contributions to an unlimited number of organizations, some of which
could be contrary to Masonic beliefs, but rather as a matter of policy that
contributions should be confined to Masonic causes or charities. Death
alone should not permit us to make donations that we are otherwise prohibited from making.
Subsequently, the Section was amended to permit donations in lieu of
flowers to Brothers who are ill and to permit donations to the California
Masonic Foundation.
It appears. under the present regulations. that much the same situation
exists as when Grand Master Warren made his original recommendation.
If a family requests a donation in lieu of flowers, other than to the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund or the California Masonic Foundation, the
Lodge is precluded from doing anything to pay tribute to its member. As
Grand Master Warren said , ''there is reason to believe that contributions
arc being made in violation of our regulations." There is also some reason
to believe, based on his original wording, that Grand Master Warren did
not intend such a restrictive regulation .
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes agrees that the present
policy can put a Lo,dge in the difficult position of uoing nothing for one
of its members, or doing something that violates the California Masonic
Code. We recommend a "Yes" vote on this Resolution.

In 1953 Section 158, Discretionary Expenditures, Ross Digest read in
part: "(Each Lodge) may in its discretion appropriate from its funds any
amount for the purchase of a testimonial for its retiring Master and for
floral pieces for an ill or deceased Brother or his family."
In 1953 Grand Master Arthur Warren in his message to the Grand
Lodge made the following comments:
"Many years ago , Grand Master Gist wisely ruled that Lodges should
not contribute to the Endowment Fund, holding that this was a voluntary
effort on the part of the Lodge . In this I heartily concur.
"The passage of time, however, has created a situation which needs
correction. In recent years it has been customary on the part of many, to
make contributions to worthy charities in lieu of floral offerings for deceased persons . Likewise, many bereft families have made the same request. There is no rule o f reason that should prohibit such a practice on
the part of our Lodges. Under our present regulations, a Lodge is prohibited from doing so, even if the family makes such a request. I have
reason to believe that contributions are being made in violation of our
regulations . The matter could be easily controlled, and rightfully so, by
the adoption of the following addition to Section No. 158 RD.
"In lieu of a floral piece for the deceased person, a contribution may
be made to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund."
The recommendation was referred to the Jurisprudence Committee
which came up with the following wording which was added to Section
158. "In lieu of a floral piece for a deceased person , when requested by
his family, a contribution may be made to the Masonic Homes Endowment

The Masonic Homes Endowment Board:
Resolution number eight has been referred to this Board for comment
and recommendation . To this assignment the Masonic Homes Endowment
Board reports the following:
It is with true compassion and understanding that the Grand Master,
supported by the Executive Committee, realized that the Brethren and
others were contributing large total sums of money to the Masonic Homes
Endowment Fund as Memorials, and caused these Memorial Contributions to be credited to the donors' respective Lodges for Honor Roll purposes. Through this type of encouragement the number and percentage
of contributors to the Endowment Fund have increased this past Grand
Lodge year, as well as the total dollar amount contributed.
It, therefore, is certainly befitting that contributions made as Memorials
by our Masonic Lodges to the Endowment Fund should also be credited
to the respective Lodges for Honor Roll purposes without the cumbersome
and often embarrassing task of obtaining "family permission."

The California Masonic Foundation Board:
Resolution No. 8 having been refe rred by the Most Wo rshipful Grand
Master to the Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Foundation for

This Board has studied the contents of said Resolution in depth over a
period of years; and initiated and recomme nded the amendment of Section
2320 to include the California Masonic Foundation therein.
This Board is of the unanimous opinion that said Resolution should be
adopted, as introduced, for the reasons therein stated and for the further
reason that we have found no justification for the inclusion of the words,
" When requested by his family," therein.
We recommend a "Yes" vote on Resolution No. 8.
Adopted.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 9 proposes to amend Section 2636 C.M.C. to allow sons
of Master Masons in good standing to petition a Lodge for degrees when
he has attained the age of eighteen.
In the ten year period 1971 through 1980, simi lar legislation has been
prop?sed five times. Some of these proposals would have lowered the age
require ment to 1_8 years for all ; some to lower the age for only Senior
DeMolays and this year, only for sons of Master Masons in good standing.
In each proposal, the argument was presented as a means of increasing
membership.
There is thus again presented the question of whether we should lower
age lin:iits to increase membership. In considering this Resolution yo ur
Com~1ttee ha~ atte'!1pted to weigh its effect on the policy of Grand Lodge.
The fust cons1derat1on must be our over-all duty and obligation to Freemasonr y.
There. are two basi~ a~d opposing beliefs on the question:
. O~e side says that institutions must change to meet the needs of changing times, that times have changed and that we must do one or more
•
things to meet the new challenge.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The other side says that we should not be discouraged by reduced membership figures , that Masonry exists to make men better and that we should
not change our qualifications for membership.
Those of the second point of view would reject any request to change
the age at which a man might apply for the degrees.
Those of the first point of view would say if there is a need. this might
be a place to make a change.
It is the opinion of your Committee that if it is desirable to reduce the
age limit for sons of Master Masons in good standing, it should also be
desirable to similarly accept all applicants of the same age. To limit the
age reduction to one special group would create two classes of applicants
and your Committee believes this to be contrary to our Masonic principles
and the policy of Grand Lodge.
Further, however, there is another basic question of whether 18 year
olds are ready to absorb and understand the teachings and lessons of
Masonry and would accepting 18 year olds have a serious and adverse
effect on the Order of DeMolay whose members remain DeMolays until
the age of 21?
Your Committee has given serious and thoughtful consideration to all
of these Policy view points and recommends a " No" vote.

California Masonic Code be amended by adding the following sentence
at the end:

The proponents of this Resolution seek to entitle each recipient of a

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, the Golden Veterans Award Ceremony presents a lapel
pin and certificate to its recipients, who have maintained a minimum of
fifty years of membership in good standing , as a symbol of our esteem for
their long and faithful service; and
WHEREAS, certain other Masonic Jurisdictions award a lifetime membership in addition to a lapel pin and certificate to their recipients. And
such presentation projects an erroneous image to the attending public that
the other jurisdictions value the service of their fifty year members ~ore
highly, particularly when such awards are given side by side; and
WHEREAS , the cost to the Grand Lodge of California by presenting
a lifetime membership to its fifty year veterans through the loss of per
capita tax is believed to be an immaterial amount.

Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 10 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to entitle each recipient of a
Golden Veterans Award to the benefits of life membership in his Lodge.
To carry out the intent of the proponents, your Committee submits the
following legislation:
RESOLVED that Section 2804 of the California Masonic Code be
amended by adding at the end thereof the following:
"A m ember receiving from this Grand Lodge a G olden Veterans award
shall thereafter be deemed a life member of his Lodge, and forever
exempt from the payment of dues therein, which dues shall be deemed
remitted ; but such member shall have no interest in the life membership
fund of such Lodge."
RESOLVED FURTHER , that Annotation 2810a be deleted.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
the Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this R esolution seek to entitle each recipient of a
Golden Veterans Award to the Benefits of Life Membership in his Lodge.
The proponents state that certain other Masonic Jurisdictions award
lifetime membership in addition to the Lapel Pin and Certificate, and that

•
PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

this projects an erroneous image to the public that these jurisdictions value
the service of their fifty year members more highly than we in California
do. They also state that the loss of per capita tax is believed to be an
immaterial amount.
In 1969, two Resolutions were proposed which were similar to this one.
The first proposed that Grand Lodge adopt a policy of issuing pair-up
memberships to its 50 year members. The second would have provided
for automatic remission of dues, in advance, to all Master Masons under
this jurisdiction who have received or are entitled to receive a fifty year
button from the Grand Lodge.
Arguments against the resolution were that payment of dues is a duty
and a privilege for a member who can afford to do so. If this creates a
hardship, for any member, the Lodge may remit his dues. Concern was
also expressed about the potential loss of revenue (the argument was also
made that Lodges could remit dues for members over 75 years of age or
40 years' membership. This was later rescinded by Grand Lodge). Neither
of the resolutions was adopted.
The Golden Veterans Button, the 50 Year Certificate and the Grand
Lodge presentation ceremony are distinguished by their beauty, simplicity
and sincere respect for the fifty year member. Perhaps we should do more.
Perhaps we should not be concerned about right versus duty or dollar
impact. However, if there are reasons to do more, it seems that they should
be more sufficient than the fact that other jurisdictions do more or that
we need to correct an erroneous impression.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No"
vote.

Grand Master Haglund called upon Past Grand Master Donald G. Ingalls who was to have presented a paper at the special program the previous afternoon. Due to the constraints of time , the paper was not able
to have been delivered as scheduled, and therefore it was delivered on
Thursday Morning. Following is the message given by Past Grand Master
Donald G. Ingalls.

Does Freemasonry today keep faith with its future? In this country, Masonry
does not involve itself in politics. Let that be understood. But let us also
remember t hat Freemasonry and the character of this nation are irrevo cably
intertwined and that a threat to one is at the same time a threat to the other.
A strong Masonic Fraternity has always given much to its cou ntry and it must
be called upon today to give even more.

262

MASONIC SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITIES
My Brethren:
Consider, if you will, that what I am about to say is a summing up of this
outstanding year in Masonry and session of Grand Lodge - an overview;
a dream; a hope; even, perhaps, an old commandment re-stated, "that ye love
one another".
In the spring of 1978, I said to the Masons of this jurisdiction, "Mark it
well, Masonry grows in strength and usefulness by keeping faith with its future
as well as with its Ancient Landmarks ... for only thus does it best serve
its members and all of those who believe in the importance of the work at
hand and the work yet to come. " Today, in 1984, I stand more strongly than
ever by those words.
My Brethren, a tree, no matter how high its crown or how deep its roots,
that stands in unbending rigidity against the changing winds of time, will
at best be stunted in growth. Consider, if you will, the Constitution of these
United States. Key among the other reasons it has survived is the fact that
it is an "open-ended" creation - that is, it is conceived to bend a little.
It can be amended by the will of the people, by their States, or by a Special
Constitutional Convention. It has not stood in unbending rigidity against the
changing winds, but, without forsaking its inherent principles, has survived

263

Richard Evans, a Past President of Rotary International, pointed out
that, ''A man may have a great truth, he may make a great discovery, he may
produce a great product, and yet die without anybody being benefited by it,
if he doesn't find a way to tell it. "
In Masonry, we have a great truth! Its wisdom is a great discover y in t he
hearts and minds of men! It produces a great product: the greatest product
of all - better men! But, its great benefit to the future could just fad e away
if we don't find a way to "tell it" - to exemplify our Masonic way of life
in ways for all to see, admire and desire to emulate.
We Masons have a social responsibility and we have a duty to our neighbors.
As Grand Master Haglund has stressed t his Masonic year, we must turn certain downtrends around in our Fraternity and achieve an upward and outward growth. We cannot stand unbending to the winds of change: We cannot
forsake p rinciple, and we won't, but we can bend enough to tell our beautiful
Masonic story to the world. Why not? Isn't it a wonderful story!?
Masonry has made some changes over t he years. Here in California we have
instituted some very fine programs. T his year's Grand Master's Achievement
Award Program blueprints activities to improve lodge officer developmen t,
to attract prospective members and improve membership participation, to encourage Masonic responsibility and to promote Masonic community involvement. But the work must now be done and no one can do it but you!
An example: I believe t hat our traditional interest and participatio n in support of our public schools must be doubled or trebled. Despite improvements,
t he public schools are still in trouble, my friends! They no longer resemble
the schools that you and I attended. Take a good look at them! I believe yo u'll
agree it's past time that we reorganize our thinking about public schools and,
working through every source available, at every level of influence, d eterm ine
the changes that are needed - and then see to it that they are put into effect.
Should we Masons be bashful? Should we continue to hide our light under
a bushel? Should we remain mute? Judge Jack Levitt, our Junior G rand
Warden, throws down the gauntlet in these words: " Should we not speak out
our belief in our principles, give action to our beliefs and have the for titude
to make certain t hat our faith bears fruit ?"
We can and we do, my Brethren, look to our past with pride. Th roughout
the history of this country, men who were Freemasons have held vital positions in the fields of finance, business, the professions and the military. They
have included fourteen Presidents and eighteen Vice Presidents of the United
States, many state Governors, members of the Senate and of t he Ho use o f

264

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Representatives. Five Chief Justices were Masons, and two of these were Grand
Masters.
Worldwide, active and dedicated Masons constitute a cross-section of who's
who - Will Rogers, Charles Lindbergh, Simon Bolivar, James Boswell,
Robert Burns, Edward VII, Garibaldi, George VI, Von Goethe, Rudyard
Kipling, Haydn, Lord Kitchener, Mazzini, Mozart, Henry Ford, J. C. Penney,
Jose Rizal, Cecil J. Rhodes, Sir Walter Scott, Sibelius, Voltaire; Generals John
J. Pershing, Mark Clark, Douglas MacArthur; Personalities John Wayne,
Ernie Borgnine, Tom Mix, Harold Lloyd, Cecil B. De Mille; Astronauts Buzz
Aldrin, Gordon Cooper, Donn Eisle, Virg Grissom, Edgar Mitchell, Walt
Schirra, Tom Stafford, Paul Weitz and James Irwin - to name just a few.

As the walrus might have said to Alice, the time has come to think of many
things: to contemplate the regeneration of our Masonic and personal lives;
to arouse the living truths within ourselves and go forth as better men to share
a message of brotherly love with the world; to force a spiritual recrudescence
of our own natures so our actions, our words, and our thoughts establish
a foundation of brotherhood and service to our fellowmen.
To talk proudly of our Craft, armed with a full knowledge of our great
past and an acute awareness of our future potential; !O change public igno~ance
of Freemasonry into public recognition of its values. Do we have the fortitude
to fu lfill our social obligation?
We live in a strange time. Our world is segmented by multiple creeds, each
claiming that it alone can solve our social problems. Anarchists and revolutionaries topple states and establish dictatorships or repressive socialist systems.
Libertarians go to any length to oppose drawing a line between freedom and
license. A mad thinking is prevalent which equates social dictatorship with
democracy, invasion with liberation, and the big lie with truth.

Masons all. Our Brothers. Dedicated to their craft's highest moral principles, each making an indelible mark upon life and his society from his chosen
area of activity. Each of these men illustrated or illustrates, in his own way,
what Past Grand Master Chester R. MacPhee was talking about when he said,
"It is not sufficient to say that I am a Mason. It is not sufficient to wear
the badge. It is not sufficient to hold even the highest Masonic office. What
is required of every single Mason is his dedicated and devoted application
to high moral principles, indeed, to basic Masonry itself. "
So acting, should we not have the fortitude to make certain that our Masonic
faith bears fruit? We look to our past with pride. Now, let us look to our
future with concern and hope.
The world changes. The patterns of society shift and rearrange. The society we live in today moves faster than any other in history, from the old
to the new, from a base secured in industry, to the current field of the
production and distribution of information. But the greatest need of this society we live in today is the same strength inherent in Masonic principles and
the inspiration of the Mason's faith in God that neither time nor adversity
can diminish.
We must find the ways to pass on to our neighbors, our friends and our
nation, these precious gifts of right living which our Craft has so generously
bestowed upon us. Remember, there are two seas in the Holy Land. One is
fresh and filled with fish. Its banks are green and trees spread their branches
over it and plunge their thirsty roots into its waters. The River Jordan fills
this sea with sparkling water from the hills. Men build houses near it, and
birds their nests, and life is happier on its shores.
But, the River Jordan flows on south into another sea. Here, there is neither
fish, nor tree, nor song of birds, nor children's laughter. The air hangs heavy
above its water and neither man, nor fowl, nor beast will drink of it.
What makes this difference in these two seas fed by the same river? The
Sea of Galilee passes on that which it receives. For every drop of water that
flows in, a drop of water flows out. The other sea has no outlet, it keeps
what it gets. It stagnates and is called the Dead.
To give is to live ... and our gift to give, my Brethren, this special gift
called Masonry, is a way of life, and a wtllingness of the heart.

265

But we understand these conditions when we remember that the forces opposing the progress of humanity are always embodiments of the same three
great negatives: Ignorance, Superstition, and Fear. Ignorance is the state of
insufficient knowledge. Superstition is addiction to that which is untrue. Fear
is man's anxiety over the consequences of his own actions. It is less than strange
then, isn't it, that Masonry's teachings and lessons are diametrically opposed
to all three?
Do our friends, our neighbors, our acquaintances know these facts? Do
they know that Masonry does stand for Brotherly Love, Relief, Truth, Justice,
H ope and an abiQ.ing Faith in God's supreme law? Masons know that any
law is never real until it is inscribed in the hearts of men.
As each man unfolds his life, he inscribes upon it a code of his own. If
he is a Mason, it is a code of helpfulness, unselfistiness, harmlessness: the
rulership of one's self, of personality, of self-discipline. This is the law that
must ultimately be fulfilled - God's law. And this is the task and the purpose of our Craft.
Masons in this country are not political - but they are patriotic. They know
that America has an assignment with destiny. They know that under a
democratic concept of living, the responsibilities for progress pass to the keeping of the people.
America does have an assignment with destiny, and Freemasonry is part
o f that destiny. And while there will be troubles, tribulations, and times of
discouragement and failure, Masons know that principles do not fail! The
Mason is aware that all things created by men are mortal and destructible,
but the way destined by the Supreme Architect of the Universe is immortal
and indest ructible.
The Mason knows that as Hiram Abiff, the widow's son, rose into a new
life from his shallow grave, so does man's spiritual progress rise victoriously
from the ashes of human ruin.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Masons have an abiding faith in the future of this country of ours, and
Masons know when we speak of the future, we mean the young men and
women who will today and tomorrow take our places.

The scene is the State House at Philadelphia. W~re all familiar with the
famous names of the known Masons present. The doors are locked and a
guard posted. A group of serious-faced men stand abou.t a table o? which
lies a parchment declaring the Independence of the American Colonies from
the mother country. Each man faces the death penalty for high treason if
he signs that document. And he knows it. They all hesitate. There is a wavering among them. And then, a voice rings out from the balcony:
"Sign that parchment! Sign, if the next moment ~he gib~et's
rope is about your neck! Sign, if the next moment this hall nngs
with the clash of falling axes! Sign, by all you hopes in life or death,
as men, as husbands, as fathers, as brothers, sign your names to
the parchment, or be accursed forever! Sign, and not only for
yourselves, but for all ages, for that parchment will be the textbook of freedom, the bible of the rights of man forever.
"Nay, do not start and whisper with surprise. It is truth, your
own hea rts witness it: God proclaims it. Look at this strange band
of exiles and outcasts, suddenly transformed into a people: a handful of men, weak in arms, but mighty in God-like faith; nay, look
at your recent achievements, your Bunker Hill, your Lexington,
and then tell me, if you can, that God has not given America to
be free!
"It is not given to our poor human intellect to climb to the skies
and to pierce the council of the Almighty One. But methinks
I stand among the awful clouds which veil the brightness of
Jehovah's throne.
"Methink~ I see the recording angel come trembling up to that
throne and speak his dread message. 'Father, the old world is baptized in blood. Father, look with one glance of thine eternal eye,
and behold evermore that terrible sight, man trodden beneath the
oppressor's feet, nations lost in blood, murder and superstition,
walking hand in hand over the graves of the victims, and not a
single voice of hope to man. '
"He stands there, the angel, trembling with the record of human
guilt. But hark! The voice of God speaks from out the awful cloud:
'Let there be light again! Tell my people, the poor and oppressed,
to go out from the old world, from oppression and blood, and
build my altar in the new. '
"As I live, my friends, I believe that to be His voice! Yes, were
my soul trembling on the verge of eternity, were this hand freezing in death, were this voice choking in the last struggle, l would
still, with the last impulse of that soul, with the last wave of that
hand, with the last gasp of that voice, implore you to remember
this truth - God has given America to be free!
"Yes, as I sank into the gloomy shadows of the grave, with my
last faint whisper I would beg you to sign that parchment for the
sake of those millions whose very breath is now hushed in intense
expectation as they look up to you for the awful words, 'YOU ARE
FREE.'"

266

It is a Masonic responsi bility to strive with all our strength and intelligence
to make certain these young people have the chance to be wiser than we are,
better than we are, and st ronger in mind and character than we are. They
are the ones who must build a new society, plumb the depths of the oceans,
and follow the trackless paths of the comets into tomorrow. They are the ones
who must take man's fin al steps toward the fountainhead of all wisdom, all
power and all glory.

Does your friend, your neighbor, your acquaintance, know that we feel this
way?
Masonry is wonderfully insightful. It takes into consideration man's woeful
fumbling with the eternal laws of life. It understands that it is not enough
to hopefully create a situation permitting men to give allegiance with their
minds or to serve faithfully with their bodies. No! Masonry underscores the
truth, and the truth is that man is inevitably and incurably an idealist, and
that this is the truth that shall one day set man free!
Masonry therefore sees to it that this idealistic content of man's nature is
properly nourished through its rituals and its teachings, and when this vital
human need is ultimately cared for, when all men share its benefits, then no
more will man's laws fail, treaties be broken, or the rights of man violated.
Isn't that the very fiber of Freemasonry? Do our non-Masonic friends know
this?
I would remind you, there are a few very important points to remember.
When we tell the wonderful story of Masonry, we will create an ambiance
so inviting, that men will be attracted to it. That means each of us will have
set himself up as a representative of all that Freemasonry stands for. Therefore,
there can be no room for pettiness of action, self-aggrandizement, or criticism
of Masonic Brothers so all may hear, instead of breathing council privately
into his ear. Brotherly Love, after all, is the cornerstone upon which all other
Masonic tenets balance. Masonry will rise or fall, always on the actions of
individual Masons. No Mason is exempt from this responsibility.
My Brethren, in Masonry we have a great truth . Its wisdom is a great
discovery. And it produces the greatest product of the world - good and
dedicated men. Here, in this year of 1984 - here in this land of the free,
has the time come at last for Freemasonry to step out of the shadows, once
necessary to escape persecution and to insure the preservation of its ideals,
and now to tell its wonderful story at a time when wonderful stories are woefully scarce? There are many false notions about Freemasonry. ls now, perhaps,
the time for the truth?
Let me close with this story. I found it in the works of Brother Manly Palmer
Hall, and verified its sources.
There is no real proof the hero was a Mason, yet legend has it that he was.
And whether he was or not just as we Masons are today, he was in the right
place at the right time with the right message, and his inspired thinking and
words were Masonic in character.

268

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The delegates, carried away, rushed fo rward, and Brother John Hancock
scarcely had time to affix his bold signature before the quill was grasped by
another. It was done.
The American patriots turned to express their appreciatio n to the unknown
speaker. He was not in the balcony. He was not to be found anywhere. How
he entered or left is not known. No one knows to this day who he was.
Whoever he was, he kept faith with the future, he believed in the importa nce of the work at hand and the work yet to come, and he helped give us
a nation dedicated to liberty and justice under God.
This man, one man, raised his voice in idealism and changed the course
of history. Each of us has the same rare opportunity, right now - we can
share with today's wavering men and women the idealism of Freemasonry
- a nd change the world!
One Mason can make the difference .. . YOU!

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A. M. of California:
As required by o ur Code your Committee o n Finance has reviewed the
audited financial statements presented by the Gra nd Treasurer for the
fiscal year ended June 30, 1984.
A substantial Supplemental Appropriation was necessary this year and
has been approved by your Grand Master. That appropriation , amounting
to $115 ,300, was composed largely (65 %) of two items:
One, o ve r which we had no control and amounting to $28,000, was
required to defend ourselves in a legal action in Southern California involving a Masonic Club. This type of expense is, hope fully, a non-recurring
cost.
The second item invo lves the expenses of the Elective and Appointive
Grand Lodge Officers. The $107 ,000 budget for those items was exceeded
by nearly $49,000. This is a recurring expense which has increased quite
rapidl y over the past few years; in fact, this year's actual costs have increased more than 100% over the same costs fo ur years ago.
Some reasons for these increases are as follow:
1. New activities pla nned primarily to stimulate interest in our Craft.
2. Breathing new life into apathetic Lodges through initiating non-ritualistic training of the officer corps.
3. The costs incurred by numerous requests of Constitue nt Lodges for
Grand Lodge Officers· attendance at a large va ri ety of functions.

GRAND LODGE O F CA LIFO RNIA

269

Unfortunately, our membership continues to decline. While we added
about 9,000 new members in the last few years, we lost more than 18,000.
The decline of our members hip over the past five years has exceeded 11 % .
We are now spending increasingly mo re mo ney in the G rand Lodge
each yea r while our membership declines. If this present trend continues,
the per capita tax will most certainly increase in o rder to support a smaller
and smaller membership.
According to a review of publica tio n and distribution costs for our California Freemason Magazine, the current assess ment of $1.00 will be adeq uate for the ensuing year. This is the second year in a row there has
been no increase for this most important publication.
The rate of reimbursement for the use of personal vehicles o n Grand
Lodge business will remain at $.18 per mile until this time in 1985 .
We are again indebted to the Very Worshipful John A. Sickenberger,
Grand Treasurer, for his invaluable assistance to this Committee and his
expe rt knowledge in the management of financia l affairs of the Grand
Lodge, and to Hugo Delfin, our Accounting Manage r, for a job well done.
Also, o ur thanks to the Very Wo rshipful Robert A . Klinger, G rand
Secreta ry. and his staff for their fine assistance.
As in the past, all Lodges were provided with ad vance notice of the
proposed per capita assessment following the Committee's August budget
meeti ng with the Grand Master and the Elective Line.
